## Proposition 6.29
**Statement:** To a given straight line to apply a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure and exceeding by a parallelogrammic figure similar to a given one.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line, let ℱ be the given rectilineal figure, and let 𝒟 be the given parallelogram. Write [X] for the area of a figure X. Bisect AB at M (1.10), and on MB construct a parallelogram MBRS similar to 𝒟 (6.18). Denote this parallelogram, also named SRBM, by Q. We shall construct a larger similar parallelogram and use its equal complements; this makes the required excess appear directly.

**Step 2.** Construct a parallelogram equal to ℱ (1.45), and adjoin it externally to Q along a nonzero boundary segment, with their interiors disjoint. Their union is a rectilineal figure 𝒢 satisfying [𝒢] = [Q] + [ℱ] (CN2).

**Step 3.** By 6.25 construct a parallelogram similar to Q and equal to 𝒢. Set a copy of it in the angle RSM, calling it STUV, with its corresponding sides ST and SV on the rays SR and SM respectively. This setting is constructed by copying the adjacent side-lengths onto the rays and completing parallels (P2, 1.3, 1.31). Corresponding angles agree by 1.29; joining the diagonals between the endpoints of those adjacent sides gives equal triangles by 1.4, and hence equal parallelograms by 1.34 and CN2 (P1). Thus STUV is similar and similarly situated to Q, and [STUV] = [Q] + [ℱ] (6.25, CN1).

**Step 4.** Similarity gives ST:SV = SR:SM (D6.1). Consequently ST compares with SR in the same way that SV compares with SM (5.14). If ST were no greater than SR, then SV would be no greater than SM, and STUV would be contained in Q or coincide with it. It could not then have greater area than Q (CN5). But [STUV] = [Q] + [ℱ] > [Q] (CN5). Therefore ST > SR and SV > SM: R lies between S and T, M lies between S and V, and Q lies within STUV.

**Step 5.** Join SU (P1). Since Q is similar and similarly situated to STUV and has the common angle at S, it is about the same diagonal SU; hence B lies on SU (6.26). Produce MB beyond B to meet TU at X, and RB beyond B to meet VU at Y (P2). The parallel sides of the two parallelograms give the resulting parallel grid (1.30). In particular, M, B, X occur in that order, and the four parts of STUV are Q, RTXB, MBYV, and BXUY.

**Step 6.** Through A draw a parallel to TU, meeting VU produced beyond V at Z (1.31, P2). Then AXUZ is a parallelogram, partitioned into the three parallelograms AMVZ, MBYV, and BXUY; their opposite sides are parallel by construction and 1.30. Its base AX contains AB and extends beyond B to X.

**Step 7.** In STUV, the parallelograms Q and BXUY are about the diagonal SU. The other two parts, RTXB and MBYV, are therefore its complements, so [RTXB] = [MBYV] (1.43).

**Step 8.** Since AM = MB, the parallelograms AMVZ and MBYV have equal bases and lie between the same parallels AB and ZU. Hence [AMVZ] = [MBYV] (1.36), and therefore [AMVZ] = [RTXB] (CN1). Here 1.36 is the natural first choice: equal bases between the same parallels already give the required equality, without a proportional-area argument.

**Step 9.** Subtract Q from the equality [STUV] = [Q] + [ℱ]. The partition in Step 5 gives
[ℱ] = [RTXB] + [MBYV] + [BXUY] (CN3).
Replace RTXB by the equal parallelogram AMVZ from Step 8. By addition of equals and the partition in Step 6,
[ℱ] = [AMVZ] + [MBYV] + [BXUY] = [AXUZ] (CN2, CN1).

**Step 10.** The parallelograms BXUY and Q are about the diagonal of STUV, and are therefore similar to one another (6.24). Since Q is similar to 𝒟, BXUY is similar to 𝒟 (6.21). The line BY separates AXUZ into the parallelogram ABYZ on the given line AB and the excess BXUY beyond B. Thus AXUZ is a parallelogram equal to ℱ, applied to AB and exceeding by a parallelogram similar to the given one, as required.

## Proposition 6.30
**Statement:** To cut a given finite straight line in extreme and mean ratio.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given finite straight line. By 2.11, cut AB at an interior point C so that the rectangle contained by AB and CB equals the square on AC. This rectangle–square construction is the direct route because it supplies exactly the equality needed for a three-term proportion. [2.11]

**Step 2.** By the converse of 6.17, applied with AB and CB as the extremes and AC as the mean,
AB : AC = AC : CB.
The three-line criterion applies directly because the given rectangle equals a square on the mean. [6.17]

**Step 3.** Since AC is a proper part of AB, AB > AC. In the proportion just obtained, the first magnitude therefore exceeds the third; hence the second exceeds the fourth. Thus AC > CB. [CN5, 5.14]

**Step 4.** Consequently, as the whole AB is to the greater segment AC, so is AC to the less segment CB. Therefore AB has been cut at C in extreme and mean ratio, as required. [D6.3]

## Proposition 6.31
**Statement:** In right - angled triangles the figure on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the similar and similarly described figures on the sides containing the right angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be right-angled at A. Denote by F_BC, F_AB, and F_AC the areas of the similar and similarly described rectilineal figures on BC, AB, and AC, respectively; these supporting sides are corresponding sides (D6.1). Path choice: transfer the established equality for squares to the given figures by the general polygon-ratio theorem.

**Step 2.** Describe squares on BC, AB, and AC, and denote their areas by Q_BC, Q_AB, and Q_AC (1.46). These squares are similar: their angles are equal right angles, and their corresponding sides are proportional because all the sides within each square are equal (D1.22, P4, D6.1).

**Step 3.** By 6.20, each of the ratios F_AB : F_BC and Q_AB : Q_BC is the duplicate ratio of AB : BC. Likewise, each of F_AC : F_BC and Q_AC : Q_BC is the duplicate ratio of AC : BC. Therefore, by 5.11,
F_AB : F_BC = Q_AB : Q_BC,
and
F_AC : F_BC = Q_AC : Q_BC.
Here 6.20 is the natural choice because the given figures are arbitrary polygons, not necessarily triangles.

**Step 4.** Adding the antecedents in these two proportions, while retaining their respective common consequents, gives
(F_AB + F_AC) : F_BC = (Q_AB + Q_AC) : Q_BC
(5.24).

**Step 5.** Since ABC is right-angled at A, the square on BC equals the squares on AB and AC together:
Q_AB + Q_AC = Q_BC
(1.47). Substitution into Step 4 therefore gives

## Proposition 6.32
**Statement:** If two triangles having two sides proportional to two sides be placed together at one angle so that their corresponding sides are also parallel, the remaining sides of the triangles will be in a straight line.

**Step 1.** Label the triangles ABC and DCE in their prescribed adjoining placement at C, with AB:AC = DC:DE, AB parallel to DC, and AC parallel to DE. In this placement CA lies inside angle BCD, and CB and CE lie on opposite sides of CD. We must prove that BC and CE form one straight line. [Given proportionality and placement.]

**Step 2.** Since AB is parallel to DC, the transversal AC gives ∠BAC = ∠ACD. Since AC is parallel to DE, the transversal CD gives ∠ACD = ∠CDE. Hence ∠BAC = ∠CDE. [1.29, CN1]

**Step 3.** The triangles ABC and DCE therefore have equal included angles and proportional sides about those angles. They are consequently equiangular, and in particular ∠ABC = ∠DCE, these angles being opposite the corresponding sides AC and DE. The direct choice is 6.6, because precisely its included-angle and two-side hypotheses have now been established. [6.6]

**Step 4.** Since AB is parallel to DC, the transversal BC makes the interior angles ABC and BCD on the same side together equal to two right angles. Thus ∠ABC + ∠BCD equals two right angles. [1.29]

**Step 5.** Add ∠BCD to the equal angles ∠ABC and ∠DCE from Step 3. Using Step 4, it follows that ∠DCE + ∠BCD equals two right angles. [CN2, CN1]

**Step 6.** At C, the straight lines CB and CE lie on opposite sides of CD and make with it the adjacent angles BCD and DCE, whose sum is two right angles. Therefore CB and CE are in a straight line. Thus the remaining sides BC and CE of the two triangles form one straight line, as required. [1.14]

## Proposition 6.33
**Statement:** In equal circles angles have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.

**Step 1.** Let θ and φ be angles in two equal circles, either both at their centres or both at their circumferences, and let a and b be the respective arcs on which they stand (D3.9). We use 3.26 directly: it converts equal angles into equal intercepted arcs in both cases, so it naturally applies to subdivisions obtained by angle-bisection. We shall establish the required proportion by the equimultiple criterion D5.5.

**Step 2.** First, comparisons between such angles agree with comparisons between their intercepted arcs. Equal angles intercept equal arcs by 3.26. If one angle is greater than another, construct an angle equal to the smaller inside the greater, sharing one boundary side (1.23), and extend its other side to the circumference (P2). Its intercepted arc is a proper part of the arc intercepted by the greater angle, and equals the arc intercepted by the smaller angle (3.26). The greater angle therefore intercepts the greater arc (CN5). Interchanging the angles gives the corresponding assertion for a smaller angle. Thus greater, equal, and smaller angles intercept respectively greater, equal, and smaller arcs.

**Step 3.** Let m and n be arbitrary positive whole-number multipliers. Choose a power of two k not smaller than either m or n. By repeated bisection, divide each of θ and φ into k equal adjacent angles, extending the dividing rays to the circumference (1.9, P2). Write θ₀ and φ₀ for one small angle in the respective divisions. The corresponding k successive arcs in each circle are equal, since their angles are equal (3.26); write a₀ and b₀ for one arc in the respective divisions. Hence, by the definition of a multiple,
θ = kθ₀, φ = kφ₀, a = ka₀, and b = kb₀ (D5.2).

**Step 4.** Take the first m adjacent small angles within θ and the first n within φ. Denote the resulting angles by Θ and Φ, and their intercepted arcs by A and B. Then
Θ = mθ₀, Φ = nφ₀, A = ma₀, and B = nb₀ (D3.9, D5.2).
Because m and n are at most k, these auxiliary angles and arcs remain within the original angles and arcs. They therefore are genuine angles of the chosen kind, standing on the indicated arcs. By Step 2, the comparison between Θ and Φ agrees with the comparison between A and B (1.23, 3.26, CN5).

**Step 5.** Taking k-fold sums and applying the addition rule for equimultiples gives
kΘ = mθ, kΦ = nφ, kA = ma, and kB = nb (5.1).
Equality is preserved under this common repetition by addition of equals (CN2). Strict inequality is also preserved: the larger magnitude consists of the smaller together with a positive remainder, and repeating both leaves a positive repeated remainder (5.1, CN5). Consequently, according as Θ exceeds, equals, or falls short of Φ, both mθ compared with nφ and ma compared with nb have that same relation. Thus mθ and nφ alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of ma and nb respectively taken in corresponding order. These unrestricted multiples are sums; they need not fit within a single angle or circumference.

**Step 6.** Since m and n were arbitrary, D5.5 gives θ : φ = a : b. The construction and comparison apply both when the two angles stand at the centres and when they stand at the circumferences. Therefore, in equal circles, angles have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand, in either case.

## Proposition 7.1
**Statement:** Two unequal numbers being set out, and the less being continually subtracted in turn from the greater, if the number which is left never measures the one before it until an unit is left, the original numbers will be prime to one another.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the unequal numbers, with A greater than B. Consider the prescribed succession of subtractions, which by hypothesis reaches a unit u without an earlier remainder measuring its predecessor. We take the direct route through the definition of numbers prime to one another: we will exclude any common measure that is a number. [Hypothesis; D7.12]

**Step 2.** Suppose, for a contradiction, that a number d measures both A and B. Thus each of A and B consists of a whole collection of copies of d. [D7.5]

**Step 3.** Consider any individual subtraction in the prescribed process, and suppose that d measures both the greater quantity X and the lesser quantity Y. Write each as a collection of whole copies of d. The collection making X must contain more copies: equally many copies would give equal totals by repeated addition of equals, and fewer copies would give a smaller total. Remove from the collection making X exactly as many copies as make Y. By subtraction of equals, the copies left have total X − Y. Since X is greater than Y, at least one copy remains. Consequently d measures the remainder X − Y. [D7.5; CN2; CN5; CN3]

**Step 4.** Initially d measures both numbers by Step 2. After each subtraction, it still measures the unchanged quantity and, by Step 3, also the remainder. Interchanging their roles does not alter this fact. Applying Step 3 successively through the given process therefore shows that d measures its final remainder, the unit u. [Hypothesis; Steps 2–3]

**Step 5.** But d, being a number, is a multitude of units, whereas u is one unit; hence d is greater than u. A positive collection of whole copies of d is either equal to d or greater than d, and therefore cannot equal u. Thus d cannot measure u, contradicting Step 4. [D7.1; D7.2; CN5; D7.5]

**Step 6.** Therefore no number measures both A and B. The unit does measure each, since every number is composed of units. Hence A and B have an unit alone as a common measure, and so the original numbers are prime to one another. [D7.2; D7.12]

## Proposition 7.2
**Statement:** Given two numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the given numbers, not prime to one another, and arrange them so that A is not less than B. If A = B, take B. If A > B and B measures A, again take B. In either case B measures both numbers, and no number greater than B can measure B: a measure occurs as one or more whole copies within what it measures. Thus B is the greatest common measure in these cases. [D7.2, D7.3, CN5]

**Step 2.** Suppose, then, that A > B and B does not measure A. Path choice: use successive subtraction, the procedure addressed directly by the immediately preceding proposition, 7.1. Starting with the pair (A, B), proceed as follows. For a current pair (x, y), with x > y, stop if y measures x. Otherwise subtract y repeatedly from x until a positive remainder z less than y is left. Record that x consists of the removed copies of y together with z, and continue with the pair (y, z). Each such subtraction is possible by removing the corresponding units; since y does not measure x, the final remainder is not empty. [7.1, D7.2, D7.3, CN3, CN5]

**Step 3.** This procedure must terminate. Whenever it continues, the lesser member strictly decreases, losing at least one unit; there cannot be more such decreases than there are units in B. Nor can the procedure first terminate with an unit: if no preceding remainder measures its predecessor until an unit is left, 7.1 says that A and B are prime to one another, contrary to the hypothesis. Hence it terminates with a number d, not an unit, which measures the preceding number C. [D7.2, CN5, 7.1, D7.12]

**Step 4.** The number d measures both original numbers. At the terminal pair it measures C and itself. Now retrace the recorded stages. At any stage, the earlier greater number x consists of some whole copies of y together with the remainder z. If d measures y and z, replace each of those copies of y, and z itself, by their constituent copies of d. Adding these copies shows that d measures x also. Applying this reasoning successively backwards from (C, d) proves that d measures A and B. [D7.2, D7.3, CN2]

**Step 5.** Let e be any number measuring both A and B. Follow the same subtraction procedure forwards. Whenever e measures x and y, both consist of whole copies of e. Subtracting y from x removes exactly the copies of e constituting y, so the remainder also consists of whole copies of e. Consequently e continues to measure every remainder throughout the procedure. In particular, e measures the terminal number d. [D7.2, D7.3, CN3]

**Step 6.** Since e measures d, it cannot be greater than d: one copy equals d, or several copies compose d and each is less than the whole. Thus every common numerical measure of A and B is at most d. By Step 4, d is itself a common measure, so d is their greatest common measure. The prescribed finite procedure therefore finds the required greatest common measure. [D7.3, CN5]

## Proposition 7.3
**Statement:** Given three numbers not prime to one another, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the three given numbers. Since they are not prime to one another, some number E, not merely the unit, measures all three. Our path is to reduce A and B while preserving their common measures, and then apply 7.2, the immediately available two-number construction, to the reduced number and C. [D7.12]

**Step 2.** Starting with the pair A, B, whenever its entries are unequal, replace the greater by its excess over the less. This preserves exactly their common measures: a measure of both old entries measures the excess, because subtracting two collections of copies of that measure leaves a collection of such copies; conversely, a measure of the excess and the unchanged entry measures their sum, which is the old greater entry. Thus both the subtraction and its reversal preserve common measures. [D7.2, D7.5, CN3, CN2]

**Step 3.** Continue until the two entries are equal, and call their common value D. This process terminates: the sum of the entries is a finite multitude of units and strictly decreases at each subtraction, while both entries remain positive. Moreover, E continues to measure both entries by Step 2, so the final D is a number, not a unit. [D7.2, CN5; Step 2]

**Step 4.** Since D measures each of the two equal final entries once, reversing the subtractions shows that D measures A and B. Conversely, every common measure of A and B measures D, by following the subtractions forward. In particular, E measures D. These conclusions also hold immediately if A and B were equal at the outset. [D7.2, D7.5, CN2, CN3; Step 2]

**Step 5.** E measures both D and C; therefore D and C are not prime to one another. By 7.2, find their greatest common measure G. This application includes the cases in which D and C are equal or one measures the other. [D7.12, 7.2; Steps 1 and 4]

**Step 6.** G measures D, and D measures A and B. Each of A and B therefore consists of copies of D, each of which in turn consists of copies of G; consequently G measures A and B. It also measures C by its construction. Thus G is a common measure of all three given numbers. [D7.5, CN2, 7.2; Steps 4 and 5]

**Step 7.** Let H be any common measure of A, B, C. Since H measures A and B, it measures D by Step 4; it also measures C. Hence H cannot exceed G, the greatest common measure of D and C. Therefore G is the greatest common measure of A, B, C, and it has been found. [7.2; Steps 4–6]

## Proposition 7.4
**Statement:** Any number is either a part or parts of any number, the less of the greater.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be arbitrary numbers, with A less than B. Choose the direct definitional route: distinguish whether A measures B, since this is precisely the distinction between “a part” and “parts” in D7.3 and D7.4.

**Step 2.** If A measures B, then A is a part of B, because the less number is a part of the greater when it measures the greater. [D7.3]

**Step 3.** If A does not measure B, then A is parts of B, because the less number is called parts of the greater when it does not measure the greater. [D7.4]

**Step 4.** Either A measures B or it does not, so these cases are exhaustive. Therefore any number is either a part or parts of any greater number, as required. [D7.3, D7.4]

## Proposition 7.5
**Statement:** If a number be a part of a number, and another be the same part of another, the sum will also be the same part of the sum that the one is of the one.

**Step 1.** Let A be a part of B, and let C be the same part of D. Thus B consists of some number n of groups each equal to A, and D consists of the same number n of groups each equal to C, where n is at least two. Denote these groups by B₁, …, Bₙ and D₁, …, Dₙ respectively. We use these groups directly, rather than introduce proportions. [Hypothesis; D7.3]

**Step 2.** Pair each group Bᵢ with the corresponding group Dᵢ. Since Bᵢ equals A and Dᵢ equals C, their sum Bᵢ + Dᵢ equals A + C. Thus each of the n paired groups equals A + C. [CN2]

**Step 3.** These n paired groups contain precisely all the units of B together with all the units of D, each occurring once. Their whole therefore coincides with, and equals, B + D. Consequently B + D consists of n groups each equal to A + C. [D7.2; CN4; Step 2]

**Step 4.** Hence A + C measures B + D exactly n times. Since n is at least two, A + C is less than B + D, and is therefore a part of it. Since A likewise measures B exactly n times, A + C is the same part of B + D that A is of B, as required. [CN5; D7.3; Steps 1 and 3]

## Proposition 7.6
**Statement:** If a number be parts of a number, and another be the same parts of another, the sum will also be the same parts of the sum that the one is of the one.

**Step 1.** Let A be parts of B, and let C be the same parts of D. Unpack the hypothesis by taking counts r<s and equal-sized groups u and v such that A consists of r copies of u and B of s copies of u, while C consists of r copies of v and D of s copies of v. Each of u and v may itself be a number or a unit. We choose direct counting of corresponding equal parts, so that unit-sized parts require no separate case. [Hypothesis; D7.1, D7.2, D7.3, D7.4.]

**Step 2.** Pair each u-group with one v-group, and call their sum w. Every such pair equals w, since adding equal u-groups to equal v-groups gives equal sums. Moreover, w is a number, being composed of at least two units. [CN2; D7.1, D7.2.]

**Step 3.** Pairing the groups constituting A and C produces exactly r copies of w; pairing those constituting B and D produces exactly s copies of w. These regroupings leave the constituent units unchanged. Hence A+C consists of r copies of w, and B+D consists of s copies of w. In particular, w is the part of B+D that measures it s times. [D7.2; CN4; D7.3.]

**Step 4.** The number A+C does not measure B+D. For suppose that B+D consisted of k copies of A+C. By Step 3, its s copies of w would then equal k blocks of r copies of w. Different counts of the same nonempty group cannot have equal totals, since the larger collection contains the smaller as a proper part. Thus s would be exactly the count in k blocks of r groups. Grouping the s copies of u constituting B into those same blocks would make B consist of k copies of A, contrary to the hypothesis that A is parts, rather than a part, of B. [CN5; D7.2, D7.4.]

**Step 5.** Since r<s, A+C is less than B+D; and, by Step 4, it does not measure B+D. It is therefore parts of B+D. More precisely, Step 3 shows that it comprises r of the s equal parts of B+D, exactly as A comprises r of the s equal parts of B. Therefore A+C is the same parts of B+D that A is of B, as required. [CN5; D7.3, D7.4.]

## Proposition 7.7
**Statement:** If a number be that part of a number, which a number subtracted is of a number subtracted, the remainder will also be the same part of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.

**Step 1.** Let A be a part of B, and let C and D be subtracted from A and B respectively, where C is the same part of D that A is of B. Write R = A − C and S = B − D. By the meaning of the same part, B consists of k copies of A and D consists of k copies of C, for the same count k greater than one. We use this measuring count directly, since the hypothesis supplies it without any conversion to ratios. [D7.3]

**Step 2.** Each copy of A consists of a copy of C together with a copy of R. Let T consist of k copies of R. Adding these decompositions over the k copies of A, the whole B equals the k copies of C together with T. The k copies of C constitute D; therefore B = D + T. [CN2]

**Step 3.** Subtract D from both sides of B = D + T. The remainders are equal, so S = T. Thus S consists of k copies of R. Since k is greater than one, R is less than S. [CN3, CN5]

**Step 4.** Consequently R measures S exactly as many times as A measures B. Therefore the remainder R is the same part of the remainder S that the whole A is of the whole B, as required. [D7.3]

## Proposition 7.8
**Statement:** If a number be the same parts of a number that a number subtracted is of a number subtracted, the remainder will also be the same parts of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.

**Step 1.** Let A be the same parts of B that C is of D, with C subtracted from A and D from B. Write E = A − C and F = B − D. Thus C < A and D < B; moreover, A < B and A does not measure B, since A is parts of B. [Hypothesis; D7.4]

**Step 2.** Express the same-parts hypothesis by its equal measuring pieces: there are positive quantities u and v, each a number or a unit, and the same counts r < s, such that A consists of r copies of u and B of s copies of u, while C consists of r copies of v and D of s copies of v. This says precisely that each smaller number comprises the same number of equal parts of its corresponding greater number. We use these decompositions and subtract corresponding pieces directly; this is the direct common-notion route, without introducing proportionality theorems. [Hypothesis; D7.1; D7.2; D7.3; D7.4; CN3]

**Step 3.** Since A > C and both contain r corresponding pieces, u > v. For if u = v, repeated addition would give A = C; if u < v, the r copies of u would form a proper part of the r copies of v, giving A < C. Both contradict A > C. Let w be the positive remainder after v is removed from u. [CN2; CN5; D7.2]

**Step 4.** Remove one copy of v from each of the r copies of u composing A. The total removed is C, and each remaining piece is w; consequently E consists of r copies of w. Likewise, removing one copy of v from each of the s copies of u composing B removes exactly D and leaves F consisting of s copies of w. These equalities follow by adding the corresponding equal pieces and subtracting equal totals. [CN2; CN3]

**Step 5.** Thus w measures F exactly s times, and E comprises r of these equal measuring pieces. Since r < s, E < F. The pieces composing E therefore have exactly the same count and the same measuring relation to F as the pieces composing A have to B. [D7.2; D7.3; CN5]

**Step 6.** To verify that E is parts, rather than a single measuring part, of F, suppose E measured F exactly k times. By Step 4, F would then consist both of s copies and of kr copies of the positive quantity w. These counts must be equal: otherwise the collection with fewer copies would be a proper part of the other and could not equal it. Hence s = kr. But B, consisting of s copies of u, would consequently consist of k copies of A, each containing r copies of u. This would make A measure B, contrary to Step 1. Therefore E does not measure F; and, by Step 5, E is the same parts of F that A is of B. The remainder is therefore the same parts of the remainder that the whole is of the whole. [D7.2; D7.3; D7.4; CN2; CN5]

## Proposition 7.9
**Statement:** If a number be a part of a number, and another be the same part of another, alternately also, whatever part or parts the first is of the third, the same part, or the same parts, will the second also be of the fourth.

**Step 1.** Let A be a part of B, and C the same part of D. Thus B consists of a certain finite number k of copies of A, while D consists of exactly k copies of C: this is what it means for A and C to measure B and D as the same part. [D7.2, D7.3]

**Step 2.** Consider whatever part or parts A is of C. These are the two possibilities when A is less than C. Our direct route is to add corresponding copies of A and C repeatedly, using the addition theorem appropriate to the case. [7.4]

**Step 3.** Suppose first that A is a part of C. Adding A to A and C to C gives sums having that same part-relation. Whenever sums of equally many copies have this relation, adding one further A and one further C preserves it, since the added numbers have the same part-relation as the preceding sums. Repeating this application until k copies have been included shows that B is the same part of D that A is of C. We use 7.5 because this is precisely its single-part case. [7.5]

**Step 4.** Suppose instead that A is parts of C. Adding A to A and C to C gives sums having those same parts. Whenever sums of equally many copies have this relation, adding one further A and one further C preserves it. Repeating until k copies have been included shows that B is the same parts of D that A is of C. Here 7.6 is the applicable addition theorem because the relation is one of parts. [7.6]

**Step 5.** Therefore, alternately, whatever part or parts the first number A is of the third C, the same part or the same parts the second B is of the fourth D, as required. [7.5, 7.6]

## Proposition 7.10
**Statement:** If a number be parts of a number, and another be the same parts of another, alternately also, whatever parts or part the first is of the third, the same parts or the same part will the second also be of the fourth.

**Step 1.** Let A be parts of B, and C the same parts of D. Suppose A is a part or parts of C, and hence A<C; we must establish the identical comparison of B with D. By the hypothesis of the same parts, there are counts r and s, with 1<r<s, and equal pieces u and v respectively, such that A consists of r copies of u, B of s copies of u, C of r copies of v, and D of s copies of v. Each of u and v may be a number or a unit. [D7.2, D7.3, D7.4]

**Step 2.** Put A′=A+A, B′=B+B, C′=C+C, D′=D+D, and U=u+u, V=v+v. Counting the same units in pairs, A′ consists of r copies of U, B′ of s copies of U, C′ of r copies of V, and D′ of s copies of V. Moreover, U and V are genuine numbers even when u or v is a unit. This doubling ensures that all subsequent applications of the numerical theorems have numbers as their terms. [D7.2, CN2]

**Step 3.** Since A and C contain equally many copies of u and v, respectively, A<C implies u<v: equality or the opposite inequality between the pieces would give equality or the opposite inequality between their sums. Consequently U<V and B<D, again by comparing equal counts of the respective pieces. Therefore U is either a part or parts of V. [CN2, CN5, 7.4]

**Step 4.** U is the same part of A′ that V is of C′, since each measures its respective whole r times. Likewise, U is the same part of B′ that V is of D′, since each measures its respective whole s times. We use 7.9 because these decompositions give exactly its same-part hypothesis. Applied to U, A′, V, C′, it says that A′ is the same part or parts of C′ that U is of V. Applied to U, B′, V, D′, it says that B′ is the same part or parts of D′ that U is of V. Thus the two doubled comparisons have one and the same part-or-parts description. [D7.3, 7.9, CN1]

## Proposition 7.11
**Statement:** If, as whole is to whole, so is a number subtracted to a number subtracted, the remainder will also be to the remainder as whole to whole.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the whole numbers, and let C and D be subtracted from them respectively, with A:B = C:D. Write R = A − C and S = B − D for the positive remainders. By D7.20, the hypothesis expresses the same multiple, the same part, or the same parts relation. We choose the direct numerical route: apply 7.7 to the part case and 7.8 to the parts case, reducing the multiple case to the part case.

**Step 2.** If A = B, then C = D by the given proportion and D7.20. Subtracting equals from equals gives R = S by CN3. Hence R:S = A:B by D7.20. We may therefore consider the unequal cases.

**Step 3.** Suppose A is the same part of B that C is of D. By 7.7, the remainder R is the same part of the remainder S that A is of B. Therefore R:S = A:B by D7.20.

**Step 4.** Suppose A is the same parts of B that C is of D. By 7.8, the remainder R is the same parts of the remainder S that A is of B. Therefore R:S = A:B by D7.20.

**Step 5.** Suppose A is the same multiple of B that C is of D. Then B measures A as many times as D measures C; thus B is the same part of A that D is of C (D7.3, D7.5). Apply 7.7 to these whole numbers B and A, subtracting D and C respectively. It follows that S is the same part of R that B is of A. Consequently R is the same multiple of S that A is of B (D7.3, D7.5). Hence R:S = A:B by D7.20.

**Step 6.** The cases supplied by D7.20 have all been established. Therefore (A − C):(B − D) = A:B: the remainder is to the remainder as whole to whole.

## Proposition 7.12
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in proportion, then, as one of the antecedents is to one of the consequents, so are all the antecedents to all the consequents.

**Step 1.** Let the given proportional pairs be A₁:B₁, A₂:B₂, …, Aₙ:Bₙ, and put S = A₁ + ⋯ + Aₙ and T = B₁ + ⋯ + Bₙ. By D7.20, the antecedents have throughout the same numerical relation to their corresponding consequents: the same multiple, the same part, or the same parts. We use these numerical descriptions directly, choosing the addition rule matching each case rather than passing to ratios of magnitudes. [D7.20]

**Step 2.** Suppose each Aᵢ is the same part of Bᵢ. By 7.5, A₁ + A₂ is that same part of B₁ + B₂. Applying 7.5 again to these sums and the next pair preserves the same part; continuing through the finite list shows that S is the same part of T that any Aᵢ is of Bᵢ. [7.5]

**Step 3.** Suppose instead that each Aᵢ is the same parts of Bᵢ. Proposition 7.6 gives that A₁ + A₂ is those same parts of B₁ + B₂. Repeating this application with each successive pair shows that S is the same parts of T that any Aᵢ is of Bᵢ. This is precisely the parts case, so 7.6 is the corresponding addition rule. [7.6]

**Step 4.** Suppose each Aᵢ is the same m-fold multiple of Bᵢ. Write each Aᵢ as the sum of m copies of Bᵢ. Adding these equal decompositions and grouping corresponding copies gives S as the sum of m copies of B₁ + ⋯ + Bₙ, that is, of T. Hence S is the same m-fold multiple of T. If the common relation is equality, then Aᵢ = Bᵢ for every i, and adding these equalities gives S = T. [D7.15; CN2; D7.20]

**Step 5.** Thus, in every case, S has to T the same numerical relation that any chosen antecedent Aᵢ has to its corresponding consequent Bᵢ. By the definition of numerical proportion, Aᵢ:Bᵢ = S:T. Therefore, as one of the antecedents is to its consequent, so are all the antecedents together to all the consequents together. [D7.20]

## Proposition 7.13
**Statement:** If four numbers be proportional, they will also be proportional alternately.

**Step 3.** Suppose A is the same parts of B that C is of D. By 7.10, alternately, whatever parts or part A is of C, B is the same parts or part of D. Therefore again A:C = B:D. [7.10, D7.20]

**Step 4.** Suppose A is the same multiple of B that C is of D. If this is the onefold case, then A = B and C = D, so A:C = B:D by substitution. Otherwise B measures A as many times as D measures C; thus B is the same part of A that D is of C. Applying 7.9 to B, A, D, C gives B:D = A:C, which is the required equality read in the opposite order. [D7.5, D7.3, 7.9, D7.20]

**Step 5.** The cases in D7.20 are exhausted, and in every case A:C = B:D. This compares antecedent with antecedent and consequent with consequent, so the four numbers are proportional alternately. [D7.20, D5.12]

## Proposition 7.14
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please, and others equal to them in multitude, which taken two and two are in the same ratio, they will also be in the same ratio ex aequali.

**Step 1.** Let A₁, …, Aₙ and B₁, …, Bₙ be two lists of numbers equal in multitude, with n ≥ 2, such that, for every i < n,
Aᵢ : Aᵢ₊₁ = Bᵢ : Bᵢ₊₁.
We must prove A₁ : Aₙ = B₁ : Bₙ, which is the asserted proportion ex aequali. [Hypothesis; D5.17]

**Step 2.** Choose numerical alternation, since it applies directly to the given proportions without translating them into proportions of magnitudes. Applying 7.13 to each proportion in Step 1 gives
Aᵢ : Bᵢ = Aᵢ₊₁ : Bᵢ₊₁
for every i < n. [7.13]

**Step 3.** By the definition of numerical proportion, these equalities say that each Aᵢ has the same multiple, part, or parts relation to Bᵢ as Aᵢ₊₁ has to Bᵢ₊₁. Repeatedly transmitting this sameness along the finite chain yields
A₁ : B₁ = Aₙ : Bₙ. [D7.20; CN1]

**Step 4.** Applying numerical alternation once more gives
A₁ : Aₙ = B₁ : Bₙ.
Thus the first number is to the last in the first list as the first is to the last in the second list: the numbers are in the same ratio ex aequali, as required. [7.13; D5.17]

## Proposition 7.15
**Statement:** If an unit measure any number, and another number measure any other number the same number of times, alternately also, the unit will measure the third number the same number of times that the second measures the fourth.

**Step 1.** Let e be the unit, and let A, B, C be the second, third, and fourth terms respectively. Suppose e measures A exactly r times and B measures C exactly r times. Thus A consists of r units, while C consists of r groups each equal to B. We take the direct path of regrouping units, without treating the unit as a number. (Hypothesis; D7.1, D7.2.)

**Step 2.** Let B consist of s units; thus e measures B exactly s times. In each of the r groups composing C, list these s units in order. This gives r rows, each containing s units; the rows merely record the unit-decompositions of the given groups. (D7.2.)

**Step 3.** For each position in a row, collect the unit occupying that position from every row. Each resulting column contains exactly r units, and therefore equals A: its units equal the corresponding units of A, so their sums are equal. There are exactly s such columns. (D7.2; CN2, repeatedly applied.)

**Step 4.** Every unit of C belongs to exactly one column, and every unit in a column belongs to C. Consequently the columns together coincide with the original collection of units composing C, and their total equals C. Since each column equals A, C is therefore the sum of exactly s copies of A. (CN4; CN2.)

**Step 5.** Hence A measures C exactly s times, while e measures B exactly s times. Thus, alternately, the unit measures the third term the same number of times that the second measures the fourth, as required. (D7.2, D7.3; Steps 2 and 4.)

## Proposition 7.16
**Statement:** If two numbers by multiplying one another make certain numbers, the numbers so produced will be equal to one another.

**Step 4.** Consequently, C and D are each composed of the same number of copies of A. Adding these equal copies term by term gives equal wholes, so C = D. Therefore the numbers produced by the two numbers multiplying one another are equal. [CN2]

## Proposition 7.18
**Statement:** If two numbers by multiplying any number make certain numbers, the numbers so produced will have the same ratio as the multipliers.

**Step 1.** Let the numbers A and B, by multiplying the same number C, produce D and E respectively. Thus D is obtained by taking C as many times as there are units in A, and E by taking C as many times as there are units in B. We must prove D:E = A:B. [D7.15]

## Proposition 7.19
**Statement:** If four numbers be proportional, the number produced from the first and fourth will be equal to the number produced from the second and third; and, if the number produced from the first and fourth be equal to that produced from the second and third, the four numbers will be proportional.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be the four numbers in their given order. Form E = AD, F = BC, and G = BD, with the left-hand factor multiplying the right-hand factor in each product. These products are understood as repeated additions. [D7.15] Our path is to compare both E and F with the auxiliary number G, avoiding any interchange of factors.

**Step 2.** Since A and B multiply the same number D to produce E and G, respectively,
A : B = E : G.
Here 7.18 applies directly because the common factor D is the number multiplied. [7.18]

**Step 3.** Since B multiplies C and D to produce F and G, respectively,
C : D = F : G.
Here 7.17 applies directly because the common factor B is the multiplier. [7.17]

**Step 4.** First suppose that the four numbers are proportional, so that A : B = C : D. [D7.20] Combining this hypothesis with Steps 2 and 3, ratios equal to the same ratio are equal to one another; hence
E : G = F : G. [5.11]

**Step 5.** Things having the same ratio to the same thing are equal. Therefore E = F, that is, AD = BC: the product of the first and fourth equals the product of the second and third. [5.9]

**Step 6.** Conversely, suppose that AD = BC, so E = F. Equal quantities have the same ratio to the same quantity; therefore
E : G = F : G. [5.7]

**Step 7.** Combining Step 6 with the identities established in Steps 2 and 3 gives A : B = C : D. [5.11] Thus the four numbers are proportional. [D7.20] Both implications are proved.

## Proposition 7.20
**Statement:** The least numbers of those which have the same ratio with them measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the greater the greater and the less the less.

**Step 1.** Let a and b be the least numbers having their ratio, and let A and B be any numbers such that a:b = A:B. By leastness, a ≤ A and b ≤ B. We use alternation because the hypothesis is already a proportion; this directly compares each least number with its corresponding number. [Hypothesis; D7.20.]

**Step 2.** By alternation, a:A = b:B. If a = A, this proportion gives b = B, and each least number measures its corresponding number once. It therefore remains to consider a < A. [7.13; D7.20.]

**Step 3.** Since a < A, a is either a part or parts of A. Suppose that a does not measure A. Then a is parts of A, and, because a:A = b:B, b is the same parts of B. [7.4; D7.3; D7.4; D7.20.]

**Step 4.** Unpacking “the same parts,” there are equal component parts e of A and corresponding equal component parts f of B such that A and B contain the same number of their respective component parts, while a and b each comprise the same number r of their respective component parts. Here r is greater than one: otherwise a would itself be one of the equal parts measuring A, contrary to the supposition. Consequently, e measures a exactly as many times as f measures b. [D7.3; D7.4; D7.20.]

**Step 5.** Hence e:a = f:b, and alternation gives e:f = a:b. But e < a and f < b, since each is one component of a whole containing more than one such component. Thus e and f are smaller corresponding terms having the ratio of a and b, contrary to their leastness. The supposition in Step 3 is therefore impossible, so a measures A. [D7.20; 7.13; CN5; leastness hypothesis.]

**Step 6.** Since a measures A, a is a part of A. From a:A = b:B, b is the same part of B, so b measures B exactly as many times as a measures A. Therefore the least numbers measure every pair having their ratio the same number of times, the greater the greater and the less the less. [D7.3; D7.20.]

## Proposition 7.23
**Statement:** If two number be prime to one another, the number which measures the one of them will be prime to the remaining number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be numbers prime to one another, and let C measure A. Thus the unit alone measures A and B in common. We use this defining common-measure criterion directly, rather than passing through proportions. [D7.12]

If either measurement is an equality, the corresponding sum simply has one copy. [D7.5, CN2]

**Step 4.** Consequently D measures both A and B, although D is not the unit. This contradicts their being prime to one another. Therefore C and B are prime to one another, as required. [D7.12]

## Proposition 7.27
**Statement:** If two numbers be prime to one another, and each by multiplying itself make a certain number, the products will be prime to one another; and, if the original numbers by multiplying the products make certain numbers, the latter will also be prime to one another [and this is always the case with the extremes].

These are successive multiplications in the sense of D7.15. Primality to one another is symmetric, since it means having the unit alone as a common measure. [D7.15, D7.12]

**Step 2.** Path choice: use 7.24, the earlier product rule, throughout, because it applies unchanged at every successive multiplication. Initially B₁ is prime to A by hypothesis. Whenever Bᵣ is prime to A, both B and Bᵣ are prime to A; therefore their product Bᵣ₊₁ is prime to A. Starting from B₁ and repeating this inference shows that every Bₙ is prime to A. The rule also applies when the two factors are equal, as at the first multiplication. [7.24]

**Step 3.** Fix any positive index n. By Step 2 and symmetry, A is prime to Bₙ. Thus A₁ is prime to Bₙ. Whenever Aᵣ is prime to Bₙ, both A and Aᵣ are prime to Bₙ, so their product Aᵣ₊₁ is prime to Bₙ. Repeat this inference until reaching Aₙ. Consequently Aₙ and Bₙ are prime to one another. [Step 2, D7.12, 7.24]

**Step 4.** Taking n = 2, the products A₂ = A·A and B₂ = B·B are the squares of the original numbers and are prime to one another. Taking n = 3, the products A₃ = A·A₂ and B₃ = B·B₂ are their cubes and are likewise prime to one another. Since n in Step 3 was arbitrary, the corresponding successive powers—the extremes at every stage—are always prime to one another. This proves the proposition. [Step 3, D7.18, D7.19]

## Proposition 7.28
**Statement:** If two numbers be prime to one another, the sum will also be prime to each of them; and, if the sum of two numbers be prime to any one of them, the original numbers will also be prime to one another.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the two numbers, and let S = A + B. Path choice: use the definition of numbers prime to one another directly, excluding any common measure other than the unit, rather than passing to ratios (D7.12).

**Step 2.** Suppose A and B are prime to one another. Let X be either of them and Y the other, so that S = X + Y. Suppose S and X are not prime to one another. Then some number D other than the unit measures both S and X (D7.12). Thus S and X each consist of whole copies of D, allowing a single copy when the measured number equals D (D7.2, D7.5). Since S is greater than X (CN5), remove from the copies constituting S as many copies as constitute X. The remaining copies constitute S − X = Y (CN3). Consequently D measures Y as well as X, contradicting that A and B are prime to one another (D7.12). Therefore S is prime to X; since X was either summand, S is prime to each of A and B (D7.12).

**Step 3.** Conversely, suppose S is prime to one summand, which we call X, and call the other summand Y. If X and Y were not prime to one another, some number D other than the unit would measure both (D7.12). Each would therefore consist of whole copies of D (D7.2, D7.5). Adjoining the copies constituting X to those constituting Y gives whole copies of D constituting X + Y = S (CN2). Hence D would measure both S and X, contrary to their being prime to one another (D7.12). Thus the original numbers A and B are prime to one another.

**Step 4.** Therefore, if two numbers are prime to one another, their sum is prime to each; and if their sum is prime to either one, the original numbers are prime to one another, as required (D7.12).

## Proposition 7.29
**Statement:** Any prime number is prime to any number which it does not measure.

**Step 1.** Let A be a prime number, and let B be a number which A does not measure. We use the direct common-measure route: primality restricts the measures of A, while being prime to B is defined by their common measures. [D7.11, D7.12]

**Step 2.** The unit measures both A and B, since each number is a multitude composed of units. [D7.2]

**Step 3.** Suppose that a number C greater than the unit measures both A and B. Since A is prime, C cannot be a measure smaller than A; consequently C must be A itself. But C measures B, so A would measure B, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus no number greater than the unit measures both A and B. [D7.11; hypothesis]

**Step 4.** Therefore A and B have the unit alone as a common measure, and hence are prime to one another. Thus any prime number is prime to any number which it does not measure. [Steps 2–3; D7.12]

## Proposition 7.30
**Statement:** If two numbers by multiplying one another make some number, and any prime number measure the product, it will also measure one of the original numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A and B multiply one another to produce C, and let a prime number p measure C. Suppose, for a contradiction, that p measures neither A nor B. [Hypotheses; assumption for contradiction.]

**Step 2.** Since p is prime and does not measure A, it is prime to A; likewise, it is prime to B. Thus A and B are each prime to p, since having only the unit as a common measure is a symmetric relation. [7.29; D7.12.]

**Step 3.** Therefore the product C of A and B is also prime to p. We choose the product-coprimality route because the conclusions of Step 2 give exactly the hypotheses of 7.24, without requiring a proportion construction. Consequently, the unit alone is a common measure of C and p. [7.24; D7.12.]

**Step 4.** But p measures C by hypothesis and measures itself once. Hence p is a common measure of C and p, and, being a number—a multitude of units—it is not the unit. This contradicts Step 3. The supposition that p measures neither factor is therefore false: p measures A or B, as required. [Hypothesis; D7.2; D7.12.]

## Proposition 7.31
**Statement:** Any composite number is measured by some prime number.

**Step 1.** Let A be a composite number. By D7.13, A has a numerical measure B; as a proper part of A, B is less than A (D7.3, CN5). Here a numerical measure is greater than the unit, since a number is a multitude of units (D7.2).

**Step 2.** Path choice: choose the least numerical measure of A by finite inspection. Inspect the numbers consisting of two units, three units, and so on, up to the numbers less than A. This inspection is finite because A is a multitude of units (D7.2), and it encounters a measure by Step 1. Let p be the first measure encountered. Thus p measures A, and no number greater than the unit and less than p measures A.

**Step 3.** Suppose p is not prime. Then p has a numerical proper measure q, rather than being measured by the unit alone (D7.11). Consequently q is greater than the unit and less than p (D7.2, D7.3, CN5).

**Step 4.** Since p measures A, A consists of a whole number of copies of p; since q measures p, each such copy consists of a whole number of copies of q (D7.5, D7.15). Replace each copy of p in A by its equal collection of copies of q. Adding these equal collections preserves the whole (CN2), so A consists entirely of copies of q. Hence q measures A (D7.5, D7.15). This contradicts the choice of p in Step 2, since q is a number less than p.

**Step 5.** Therefore p has no numerical proper measure. The unit measures p because p is composed of units (D7.2); thus p is prime (D7.11). Since p measures A by Step 2, the arbitrary composite number A is measured by a prime number, as required.

## Proposition 7.33
**Statement:** Given as many numbers as we please, to find the least of those which have the same ratio with them.

**Step 1.** Let A₁, …, Aₙ be the given numbers. Choose the common-measure route: cancel one greatest common measure, then establish minimality using the two-number results. To find this measure for an arbitrary finite list, test the unit and every number not exceeding the smallest Aᵢ, retaining those which measure every Aᵢ. Each test is performed by repeated addition until the relevant Aᵢ is reached or exceeded. There are finitely many candidates, and the unit always succeeds; therefore select the greatest successful candidate, d. No greater candidate can measure the smallest entry. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.15, CN5]

**Step 2.** For each i, take Bᵢ to be the number of times d measures Aᵢ, retaining the unit if this count is one. Thus Aᵢ = dBᵢ. Simultaneous multiplication by d preserves ratios, so Bᵢ:Bⱼ = Aᵢ:Aⱼ for every pair of indices. This follows from 7.17 when the factors are numbers; cases involving the unit follow directly from the definition of numerical proportion. [D7.15, 7.17, D7.20]

**Step 3.** No number greater than the unit measures all the Bᵢ. For if e > 1 did so, write Bᵢ = eKᵢ. Grouping the repeated additions shows that Aᵢ = (de)Kᵢ; hence de would measure every Aᵢ. But de > d, since it contains more than one copy of d, contradicting the choice of d. [D7.15, CN2, CN5; Step 1]

**Step 4.** Let C₁, …, Cₙ be any other list having the same corresponding ratios as the given list. Then Bᵢ:Bⱼ = Cᵢ:Cⱼ. If some Bⱼ is the unit, these proportions say that each Cᵢ consists of Cⱼ copies of Bᵢ. Consequently Cᵢ ≥ Bᵢ for every i, and the constructed list is least in this case. [Step 2, CN1, D7.20, D7.15, CN5]

**Step 5.** It remains to consider the case in which every Bᵢ is greater than the unit. Suppose, for a contradiction, that some Cₖ < Bₖ. Alternating Bₖ:Bᵢ = Cₖ:Cᵢ gives
Bₖ:Cₖ = Bᵢ:Cᵢ
for every i. Alternation is supplied by 7.13; if a unit occurs among the Cᵢ, the same conclusion follows directly by counting the multiples specified in D7.20. [7.13, D7.20]

**Step 6.** Reduce the pair Bₖ, Cₖ by its greatest common measure g. If Cₖ is the unit, put g equal to the unit; likewise do so if the two numbers are prime to one another. Otherwise construct g by 7.2. Write Bₖ = gp and Cₖ = gq. Since Bₖ > Cₖ, we have p > q ≥ 1. Moreover, no number greater than the unit measures both p and q: such a measure h would make gh > g a common measure of Bₖ and Cₖ, exactly as in Step 3. Thus, when q is a number, p and q are prime to one another. [7.2, D7.12, D7.15, CN2, CN5; Step 3]

**Step 7.** If q is the unit, Bₖ is p times Cₖ. The proportions in Step 5 therefore make every Bᵢ p times Cᵢ. Thus p > 1 measures every Bᵢ, contradicting Step 3. [D7.20]

If q is greater than the unit, apply 7.21: p and q are the least numbers in their ratio because they are prime to one another. This is the naturally applicable least-ratio result, since coprimality has just been established. Also p:q = Bₖ:Cₖ = Bᵢ:Cᵢ, by simultaneous multiplication and Step 5. Hence 7.20 implies that p measures every Bᵢ. Again p > 1, contradicting Step 3. [7.21, 7.17, CN1, 7.20]

**Step 8.** Therefore no corresponding entry Cₖ can be smaller than Bₖ. The constructed B₁, …, Bₙ have the same ratios as the given numbers and are no greater, entry by entry, than any other list with those ratios. They are consequently the required least numbers. [Steps 2, 4–7]

## Proposition 7.34
**Statement:** Given two numbers, to find the least number which they measure.

**Step 1.** Let the given numbers be A and B. If they are equal, take that number. If one measures the other, take the latter. In either case the chosen number is measured by both and is itself one of the given numbers; no smaller number can be measured by it. Thus it is the required least number. Henceforth suppose that neither A nor B measures the other. (D7.5; CN5.)

**Step 2.** Find the least numbers a and b having the same ratio as A and B, so that A:B = a:b. This construction is supplied by 7.33. We choose the least-ratio route because 7.20 then applies directly to establish minimality.

**Step 3.** Form the product M = Ab. Since A:B = a:b, the products Ab and Ba are equal by 7.19. By commutativity of multiplication, M therefore consists both of b copies of A and of a copies of B. Consequently A and B both measure M. (D7.15; 7.16; D7.5.)

**Step 4.** Let N be any number measured by both A and B. It must exceed each: it cannot be smaller than either, and equality with either would make one of A and B measure the other, contrary to Step 1. Let x and y be the numbers of times that A and B respectively measure N. Thus Ax = N = By, using commutativity to write the products in this order. Hence Ax = By, and the converse part of 7.19 gives A:B = y:x. (D7.5; CN5; D7.15; 7.16; CN1; 7.19.)

**Step 5.** Since a and b are the least numbers in the ratio A:B, and y:x has that same ratio, a and b measure y and x respectively the same number of times. In particular, b measures x; therefore x is either equal to b or greater than b. (7.20; D7.5; CN5.)

**Step 6.** Now M consists of b copies of A, whereas N consists of x copies of A. If x = b, these equal sums give N = M. If x > b, the first b copies constitute M and the remaining copies make N greater than M. Thus every number measured by both A and B is at least M. Since both measure M by Step 3, M is the least number which the given numbers measure, as required. (D7.15; CN2; CN5.)

## Proposition 7.35
**Statement:** If two numbers measure any number, the least number measured by them will also measure the same.

**Step 1.** Let A and B measure N. By 7.34, take L to be the least number measured by both A and B. Since N is itself measured by both, L is not greater than N. **Path choice:** use the leastness of L directly through repeated subtraction, without introducing proportional numbers. [7.34]

**Step 2.** Starting with N, subtract L repeatedly whenever the remaining quantity is at least L. A number is a finite multitude of units, and each subtraction removes a positive collection of those units. Thus this process terminates, either with nothing remaining or with a nonempty remainder R less than L. This constructs the remainder directly; no division theorem is assumed. [D7.2; CN5]

**Step 3.** Every nonempty remainder in this process is measured by both A and B. Indeed, initially N consists of whole copies of A, and L also consists of whole copies of A. Whenever L is subtracted, cancel from the current grouping exactly the copies of A making up L; because the current quantity is at least L, these copies are available. The difference therefore consists of whole copies of A, unless nothing remains. The same argument, grouping separately into copies of B, applies to B. Repeating this reasoning at each subtraction proves the assertion. [D7.15; D7.5; CN3; CN5]

**Step 4.** If the terminal remainder R were nonempty, Step 3 would make it a number measured by both A and B, while Step 2 gives R less than L. This contradicts the leastness of L established in Step 1. Therefore nothing remains when the subtraction process ends. [7.34; Steps 1–3]

**Step 5.** Adding back the copies of L removed in the process reconstructs N exactly. Hence N consists of whole copies of L, so L measures N. Therefore, if two numbers measure any number, the least number measured by them also measures that same number. [CN2; D7.15; D7.5]

## Proposition 7.36
**Statement:** Given three numbers, to find the least number which they measure.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the three given numbers. By 7.34, find D, the least number measured by A and B. Thus A and B both measure D. Our path is to apply the two-number construction successively, since it applies directly to the given data. [7.34]

**Step 2.** Again by 7.34, find E, the least number measured by D and C. Thus D and C both measure E. [7.34]

**Step 3.** A and B also measure E. Indeed, E consists of copies of D, and each copy of D consists of copies of A. Replacing each copy of D by this equal sum shows that E consists of copies of A. The same reasoning applies to B. Consequently A, B, C all measure E. This argument includes a single copy whenever two of the numbers concerned are equal. [D7.5, D7.15, CN2; Steps 1–2]

**Step 4.** Let N be any number measured by A, B, C. Since A and B measure N, their least common multiple D also measures N, by 7.35. Therefore D and C both measure N. [7.35; Step 1]

**Step 5.** Since E is the least number measured by D and C, and N is measured by both, E cannot be greater than N. Thus no number smaller than E is measured by all three given numbers. Together with Step 3, this proves that E is the required least number which A, B, C measure. [7.34; Steps 2–4]

## Proposition 7.37
**Statement:** If a number be measured by any number, the number which is measured will have a part called by the same name as the measuring number.

**Step 1.** Let N be measured by M, and let u be a unit. If N equals M, then N consists of as many equal unit parts as there are units in M; a unit is therefore the required part named after M. Hence suppose M is less than N. [D7.1, D7.2]

**Step 2.** Since M measures N, N is a multiple of M. Let Q consist of as many units as there are repetitions of M in N. Since M is less than N, these repetitions are more than one, so Q is a number. Thus u measures Q the same number of times that M measures N. [D7.5, D7.2]

**Step 3.** Apply 7.15 to u, Q, M, N. Alternately, u measures M the same number of times that Q measures N. This is the direct path: 7.15 interchanges the measurement counts already obtained, without requiring a passage through products. [7.15]

**Step 4.** Therefore N consists of equal copies of Q, as many as there are units in M. Since M is a number, there is more than one such copy, and Q is less than N. [D7.2, CN5] Since Q also measures N, Q is a part of N. [D7.3] Its denomination is precisely M, because it measures N as many times as there are units in M. Thus the number measured has a part called by the same name as the measuring number.

**Statement:** If a number have any part whatever, it will be measured by a number called by the same name as the part.

# Book 8

## Proposition 8.1
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the extremes of them be prime to one another, the numbers are the least of those which have the same ratio with them.

**Step 1.** Let A₁, …, Aₙ be the given numbers in continued proportion, with A₁ and Aₙ prime to one another. Let B₁, …, Bₙ be any numbers having the same corresponding ratios, so that Aᵢ:Aᵢ₊₁ = Bᵢ:Bᵢ₊₁ for every i < n. We shall show that each Aᵢ is no greater than Bᵢ. (Hypotheses; D7.12, D7.20.)

**Step 2.** Taking the corresponding ratios ex aequali gives A₁:Aₙ = B₁:Bₙ. (7.14.) Since A₁ and Aₙ are prime to one another, they are the least numbers having their ratio. (7.21.) This is the direct path: apply the coprimality hypothesis to the extremes, without constructing a least proportional sequence.

**Step 3.** The least numbers having a given ratio measure any numbers having that ratio the same number of times. Hence A₁ measures B₁ and Aₙ measures Bₙ with the same measurement count. Write this count as k ≥ 1, so B₁ = kA₁, where k = 1 means equality. (7.20.)

**Step 4.** For any i with 2 ≤ i ≤ n, apply ex aequali to the first i terms to obtain B₁:Bᵢ = A₁:Aᵢ. (7.14.) Alternately, B₁:A₁ = Bᵢ:Aᵢ. (7.13.) Therefore Bᵢ is the same multiple of Aᵢ that B₁ is of A₁: namely, Bᵢ = kAᵢ. (D7.20.)

**Step 5.** Thus every Bᵢ consists of the same positive number k of copies of Aᵢ. If k = 1, all corresponding terms are equal; if k > 1, each Bᵢ is greater than Aᵢ, since the whole is greater than its part. (CN5.) Since the comparison sequence was arbitrary, A₁, …, Aₙ are the least numbers having the same ratios with them, as required.

## Proposition 8.2
**Statement:** To find numbers in continued proportion, as many as may be prescribed, and the least that are in a given ratio.

**Step 1.** Let A:B be the given numerical ratio, and let n ≥ 2 be the prescribed number of terms. Find the least numbers a, b having the ratio A:B, by 7.33. These numbers are prime to one another, by 7.22. If n = 2, they already give the required construction; henceforth suppose n ≥ 3.

**Step 2.** We describe a construction that adds one term while preserving the required ratio. Suppose X₀, X₁, …, Xₖ₋₁ are k numbers whose successive ratios are all a:b. By multiplication, construct the following k + 1 numbers:

 aX₀, aX₁, …, aXₖ₋₁, bXₖ₋₁.

Here aX means the number obtained when a multiplies X. Each indicated construction is repeated addition, as specified in D7.15.

**Step 3.** For every i from 0 through k − 2, the common multiplier a gives

 aXᵢ : aXᵢ₊₁ = Xᵢ : Xᵢ₊₁ = a:b,

by 7.17 and 5.11. For the final adjacent pair, the common multiplicand Xₖ₋₁ gives

 aXₖ₋₁ : bXₖ₋₁ = a:b,

by 7.18. Thus every successive ratio in the enlarged row is a:b, and therefore A:B, by 5.11 and Step 1. The row remains in continued proportion.

**Step 4.** Begin with the row a, b and perform the construction of Step 2 exactly n − 2 times. Steps 2–3 show that this produces exactly n numbers in continued proportion with successive ratio A:B. At every extension, the first term is multiplied by a and the last term by b. Consequently, the final extremes are a^(n−1) and b^(n−1), where each power denotes the product of n − 1 copies of its base, formed by repeated multiplication (D7.15).

**Step 5.** Since a and b are prime to one another, their corresponding powers a^(n−1) and b^(n−1) are prime to one another, by 7.27. Apply 8.1: numbers in continued proportion whose extremes are prime to one another are the least of those having the same ratio with them. ## Proposition 8.3
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, the extremes of them are prime to one another.

**Step 1.** Let A₀, A₁, …, Aₙ be the given numbers in continued proportion, least among all sequences having the same successive ratios. If n = 1, the extremes are prime to one another by 7.22. Assume therefore that n ≥ 2. We use a comparison progression, allowing 8.1 to be applied in its stated, forward direction.

**Step 2.** Choose the least numbers p, q such that p:q = A₀:A₁, by 7.33. Then p and q are prime to one another by 7.22. This proposition applies directly because the chosen pair is least.

**Step 3.** Form the n + 1 numbers
Bᵢ = pⁿ⁻ⁱqⁱ, for 0 ≤ i ≤ n,
where powers denote repeated multiplication and a factor with exponent zero is omitted. For each 0 ≤ i < n, put Cᵢ = pⁿ⁻ⁱ⁻¹qⁱ. Since n ≥ 2, each Cᵢ contains at least one factor. By repeated multiplication and interchange of factors,
Bᵢ = Cᵢp and Bᵢ₊₁ = Cᵢq. [D7.15, 7.16]
Therefore Bᵢ:Bᵢ₊₁ = p:q, since multiplication of two numbers by the same number preserves their ratio. [7.17] Thus B₀, B₁, …, Bₙ are in continued proportion with the same successive ratios as the given numbers. [Step 2; hypothesis]

**Step 4.** The extremes of this comparison progression are B₀ = pⁿ and Bₙ = qⁿ. Since p and q are prime to one another, their corresponding successive powers are prime to one another, by repeated application of 7.27. Hence B₀ and Bₙ are prime to one another.

**Step 5.** By 8.1, the comparison progression is least among those having its successive ratios. These are also the successive ratios of the given progression. For each i, the assumed leastness of the given progression gives Aᵢ ≤ Bᵢ, while the leastness just established gives Bᵢ ≤ Aᵢ. Consequently Aᵢ = Bᵢ for every i. [Hypothesis; 8.1]

**Step 6.** In particular, A₀ = B₀ and Aₙ = Bₙ. By Step 4 their only common measure is the unit. Therefore the extremes A₀ and Aₙ of the given progression are prime to one another, as required. [D7.12]

## Proposition 8.4
**Statement:** Given as many ratios as we please in least numbers, to find numbers in continued proportion which are the least in the given ratios.

**Step 1.** Let the given ratios, expressed in least numbers, be a₁:b₁, …, aₘ:bₘ, in the prescribed order. We seek numbers N₀, …, Nₘ such that Nᵢ₋₁:Nᵢ = aᵢ:bᵢ for every i, and which are the least satisfying these conditions. We shall first construct an integral chain with these successive ratios and then apply the general minimization construction of **7.33**. This is the direct choice because that proposition applies to an arbitrary finite list, without requiring all its successive ratios to be equal.

**Step 2.** Start with the chain a₁, b₁. Suppose that C₀, …, Cₖ has already been constructed with the first k prescribed successive ratios, where k < m. For the next ratio, write a = aₖ₊₁ and b = bₖ₊₁, and construct
Dⱼ = aCⱼ for 0 ≤ j ≤ k, and Dₖ₊₁ = bCₖ.
These products are constructed by repeated addition as in **D7.15**.

**Step 3.** For every 1 ≤ j ≤ k, multiplication by the same number preserves the ratio, so
Dⱼ₋₁:Dⱼ = Cⱼ₋₁:Cⱼ = aⱼ:bⱼ (**7.17**, **5.11**).
Also, multiplication is commutative, and therefore
Dₖ:Dₖ₊₁ = (aCₖ):(bCₖ) = (Cₖa):(Cₖb) = a:b (**7.16**, **7.17**).
Thus the new chain retains all the previous prescribed ratios and adds the next one. Repeating this construction through the finite list produces numbers U₀, …, Uₘ satisfying Uᵢ₋₁:Uᵢ = aᵢ:bᵢ for every i.

**Step 4.** Apply **7.33** to U₀, …, Uₘ, obtaining the least numbers N₀, …, Nₘ having the same ratios as that list. In particular,
Nᵢ₋₁:Nᵢ = Uᵢ₋₁:Uᵢ = aᵢ:bᵢ
for every i (**5.11**). Hence the constructed numbers have all the required successive ratios.

**Step 5.** Let T₀, …, Tₘ be any other numbers having the prescribed successive ratios. Their corresponding adjacent ratios equal those of U₀, …, Uₘ by **5.11**. For any indices r < s, apply the numerical ex aequali theorem **7.14** to the intervening chains; it gives Tᵣ:Tₛ = Uᵣ:Uₛ. Thus every competing chain belongs to the class of lists minimized in Step 4. By **7.33**, no Tᵢ is smaller than its corresponding Nᵢ. Therefore N₀, …, Nₘ are the least numbers in a continued chain having the given ratios, as required.

## Proposition 8.5
**Statement:** Plane numbers have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their sides.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be any plane numbers, with sides a, b and c, d respectively. Thus a multiplying b produces A, and c multiplying d produces B (D7.16).

**Step 2.** Let E be the number produced by c multiplying b (D7.15). Path choice: this mixed product makes the two required side ratios occur successively in the chain A, E, B, so the multiplication-ratio propositions apply directly.

**Step 3.** The numbers a and c, multiplying the same number b, produce A and E respectively. Therefore A:E = a:c, since the products have the same ratio as the multipliers (7.18). This proposition applies directly because the number multiplied is common.

**Step 4.** The same number c, multiplying b and d, produces E and B respectively. Therefore E:B = b:d, since the products have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied (7.17). This proposition applies directly because the multiplier is common.

**Step 5.** The ratio A:B is compounded of A:E and E:B: multiplying the sizes of these successive ratios cancels the common intermediate term E (D6.5). By Steps 3 and 4, these ratios are respectively a:c and b:d. Hence A:B is the ratio compounded of a:c and b:d, which are the ratios of the corresponding sides. Therefore plane numbers have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their sides.

## Proposition 8.6
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the first do not measure the second, neither will any other measure any other.

**Step 1.** Let A₀, A₁, …, Aₙ be numbers in continued proportion, and suppose that A₀ does not measure A₁. Choose arbitrary positions i < j, and put d = j − i. We shall prove that Aᵢ does not measure Aⱼ. [Hypothesis; D7.20]

**Step 2.** Construct d + 1 least terms B₀, B₁, …, B_d in continued proportion with the same consecutive ratio as the given numbers. Thus B₀:B₁ = A₀:A₁, and likewise for every consecutive pair. We choose this least-chain construction because it permits direct application of the coprimality theorem for the extremes. [8.2]

**Step 3.** B₀ cannot be the unit. For the unit measures every number, so it would measure B₁; the equality B₀:B₁ = A₀:A₁ would then imply that A₀ measures A₁, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus B₀ is not the unit. Moreover, because the B-terms are the least in their continued proportion, B₀ and B_d are prime to one another. [D7.2; D7.20; D7.3; 8.3]

**Step 4.** The chains Aᵢ, Aᵢ₊₁, …, Aⱼ and B₀, B₁, …, B_d have equally many terms and equal corresponding consecutive ratios. Therefore, ex aequali, Aᵢ:Aⱼ = B₀:B_d. We use the numerical ex aequali theorem, since all the terms here are numbers. [7.14]

**Step 5.** Suppose that Aᵢ measures Aⱼ. The proportion in Step 4 then implies that B₀ measures B_d. Since B₀ also measures itself once, B₀ is a common measure of B₀ and B_d. But B₀ is not the unit, contradicting the fact that these extremes are prime to one another. Consequently Aᵢ does not measure Aⱼ. [D7.20; D7.3; D7.12; Step 3]

**Step 6.** Since i < j were arbitrary, no earlier term measures any later term in the continued proportion. Thus, if the first does not measure the second, neither will any other measure any other in the order of the proportion. [Steps 1–5]

## Proposition 8.7
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the first measure the last, it will measure the second also.

**Step 1.** Let A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ be numbers in continued proportion, and suppose that A₁ measures Aₙ. We must show that A₁ measures A₂. [Hypothesis]

**Step 2.** Choose the direct route of applying 8.6 by contraposition, since it addresses exactly the failure of the desired conclusion. Suppose that A₁ does not measure A₂. Then, by 8.6, no term measures another later term; in particular, A₁ does not measure Aₙ. [8.6]

**Step 3.** This contradicts the hypothesis that A₁ measures Aₙ. Therefore A₁ measures A₂: the first measures the second, as required. [Steps 1–2]

## Proposition 8.8
**Statement:** If between two numbers there fall numbers in continued proportion with them, then, however many numbers fall between them in continued proportion, so many will also fall in continued proportion between the numbers which have the same ratio with the original numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A₀, A₁, …, Aₘ₊₁ be in continued proportion, with m intermediate numbers, and let C and D satisfy C:D = A₀:Aₘ₊₁. Thus all successive ratios Aᵢ:Aᵢ₊₁ are equal. We must place m numbers in continued proportion between C and D. [Hypothesis; D7.20]

**Step 2.** Construct m+2 numbers B₀, B₁, …, Bₘ₊₁ in continued proportion, the least in the ratio A₀:A₁. Then Bᵢ:Bᵢ₊₁ = Aᵢ:Aᵢ₊₁ for every successive pair. This is the least-progression route: the construction of 8.2 applies directly because there is a single repeated ratio. [8.2]

**Step 3.** Applying ex aequali to the two sequences gives B₀:Bₘ₊₁ = A₀:Aₘ₊₁, and hence B₀:Bₘ₊₁ = C:D. We use the numerical ex aequali theorem because both sequences consist of numbers. [7.14; hypothesis]

**Step 4.** Since the B-sequence is the least in its continued ratio, its extremes B₀ and Bₘ₊₁ are prime to one another. Consequently, these extremes are the least pair having their ratio. [8.3; 7.21]

**Step 5.** Because B₀:Bₘ₊₁ = C:D, the least numbers B₀ and Bₘ₊₁ measure C and D respectively the same number of times. Thus C and D are corresponding equal multiples of these extremes. [7.20]

**Step 6.** For each i, take Cᵢ to be the same multiple of Bᵢ as C is of B₀. These multiples are obtained by repeated addition; if the common multiplicity is one, retain Bᵢ itself. By Step 5, C₀ = C and Cₘ₊₁ = D. [D7.15; Step 5]

**Step 7.** Multiplication by the same number preserves the ratio of each successive pair, so Cᵢ:Cᵢ₊₁ = Bᵢ:Bᵢ₊₁ for every i; for multiplicity one these equalities hold immediately. Since the B-sequence is in continued proportion, so is C₀, C₁, …, Cₘ₊₁. Its endpoints are C and D, and its intermediate terms are exactly C₁, …, Cₘ, numbering m. Therefore the same number of means can be placed in continued proportion between any two numbers having the original endpoint ratio. [7.17; Steps 2 and 6]

## Proposition 8.9
**Statement:** If two numbers be prime to one another, and numbers fall between them in continued proportion, then, however many numbers fall between them in continued proportion, so many will also fall between each of them and an unit in continued proportion.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be prime to one another, and suppose that m numbers fall between them in continued proportion. Put n = m + 1, and write the progression as A = X₀, X₁, …, Xₙ = B, so that all consecutive ratios are equal (D7.20). By 8.1, this progression is the least among progressions of the same length and consecutive ratio. We choose this route because 8.1 applies directly to the given hypothesis that the extremes are prime to one another.

**Step 2.** Neither endpoint measures the other, since otherwise that endpoint would be a common measure greater than the unit, contrary to D7.12. Consequently, the common consecutive ratio cannot be an integral multiple in either direction: otherwise, proceeding through the progression in the appropriate direction, every term would be the same integral multiple of its predecessor, and one endpoint would measure the other (D7.15, D7.20). Choose the least numbers p and q such that p:q = X₀:X₁ (7.33). Neither term can be the unit, by the preceding observation; and p and q are prime to one another by 7.22.

**Step 3.** Form n + 1 products C₀, C₁, …, Cₙ, where Cᵢ contains n − i factors equal to p and i factors equal to q. Thus C₀ = pⁿ and Cₙ = qⁿ, with powers denoting repeated multiplication (D7.15). For each i < n, let Tᵢ be the product containing n − i − 1 factors p and i factors q. Since n ≥ 2, this product contains at least one factor. Regrouping the repeated products and commuting factors gives Cᵢ = Tᵢp and Cᵢ₊₁ = Tᵢq (D7.15, 7.16). Therefore Cᵢ:Cᵢ₊₁ = p:q by 7.17. Hence the Cᵢ form a continued proportion with the same length and consecutive ratio as the given progression.

**Step 4.** Apply the product rule 7.24 repeatedly, which handles any prescribed number of factors. Since p is prime to q, every repeated product of p is prime to q; in particular, pⁿ is prime to q. Primality to one another is symmetric (D7.12), so repeated application of 7.24 to products of q now shows that qⁿ is prime to pⁿ. Thus C₀ and Cₙ are prime to one another.

**Step 5.** By 8.1, the progression C₀, …, Cₙ is therefore also the least among progressions of this length and consecutive ratio. Both it and X₀, …, Xₙ are least in the same class, so each corresponding term is no greater than the other and hence they are equal. In particular, A = pⁿ and B = qⁿ.

**Step 6.** Let 1 denote the unit (D7.1). The sequences A = pⁿ, pⁿ⁻¹, …, p, 1 and B = qⁿ, qⁿ⁻¹, …, q, 1 are continued proportions: in the first, each term is p times its successor; in the second, each term is q times its successor (D7.15, D7.20). Each sequence has exactly n − 1 = m numbers between its endpoints. Thus, however many numbers fall between A and B in continued proportion, so many also fall between each of A and B and the unit in continued proportion, as required.
