## Proposition 8.10
**Statement:** If numbers fall between each of two numbers and an unit in continued proportion, however many numbers fall between each of them and an unit in continued proportion, so many also will fall between the numbers themselves in continued proportion.

**Step 1.** Let m numbers fall in continued proportion between each of A and B and the unit, and put n=m+1. Write the given progressions as
1=a_0, a_1, …, a_n=A,
1=b_0, b_1, …, b_n=B.
Thus each progression has n−1=m intermediate terms. Put p=a_1 and q=b_1. The successive ratios in the two progressions are respectively 1:p and 1:q. [Hypothesis; D7.20.]

**Step 2.** Since a_i:a_{i+1}=1:p, the number a_i is the same part of a_{i+1} that the unit is of p. Consequently a_{i+1} is p times a_i. Likewise b_{i+1} is q times b_i. Starting from the unit and repeating this observation, A is the product of n copies of p, and B is the product of n copies of q. [D7.2, D7.20, D7.15.]

**Step 3.** Choose the direct product construction, since Step 2 expresses both endpoints as products with the same number of factors. For every j from 0 through n, form C_j as the product of n−j copies of p and j copies of q, omitting whichever group has no factors. These are numbers, and C_0=A and C_n=B. In these products, factors may be regrouped by expanding multiplication into repeated addition and regrouping the equal summands; factors may also be interchanged. [D7.15, CN2, 7.16; Step 2.]

**Step 4.** For each j from 0 through n−1, let R_j be the product of n−j−1 copies of p and j copies of q. Since n−1=m≥1, R_j has at least one factor and is a number. Regrouping and interchanging factors gives
R_j·p=C_j and R_j·q=C_{j+1}.
Therefore C_j:C_{j+1}=p:q by 7.17, which applies directly because the same number R_j multiplies p and q. [D7.15, CN2, 7.16, 7.17.]

**Step 5.** Every successive pair in C_0, C_1, …, C_n therefore has the same ratio. Since C_0=A and C_n=B, the numbers C_1, …, C_{n−1} fall between A and B in continued proportion. Their multitude is n−1=m, exactly the multitude falling between each given number and the unit. This proves the proposition. [D7.20; Steps 1, 3–4.]

## Proposition 8.11
**Statement:** Between two square numbers there is one mean proportional number, and the square has to the square the ratio duplicate of that which the side has to the side.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be square numbers, with sides a and b respectively. Thus A = a·a and B = b·b [D7.18]. Form the number M = a·b [D7.15]. We choose this product directly as the proposed mean.

**Step 2.** Multiplying a and b by the same number a produces A and M. Therefore A:M = a:b [7.17]. The common-multiplier theorem is the direct choice because these two products share their multiplier.

**Step 3.** Multiplication in the opposite order gives b·a = a·b = M [7.16]. Hence multiplying a and b by b produces M and B, so M:B = a:b [7.17].

**Step 4.** Since A:M and M:B are both equal to a:b, they are equal to one another [5.11]. Thus A:M = M:B, and A, M, B are in continued proportion; consequently M is a mean proportional number between the two squares [D7.20].

**Step 5.** For three numbers in continued proportion, the ratio of the first to the third is duplicate of the ratio of the first to the second [D5.9]. Therefore A:B is duplicate of A:M. But A:M = a:b by Step 2 [7.17]. Hence the square A has to the square B the ratio duplicate of that which its side a has to the side b, as required.

## Proposition 8.12
**Statement:** Between two cube numbers there are two mean proportional numbers, and the cube has to the cube the ratio triplicate of that which the side has to the side.

**Step 1.** Let C and D be the given cube numbers, with sides a and b. Write xy for the number obtained when x multiplies y. Put p = aa, q = ab, and r = bb; then C = ap and D = br. Construct M = aq and N = ar. These are numbers obtained by multiplication. We choose this direct construction because it exhibits the required means explicitly. [D7.15, D7.19]

**Step 2.** Since a multiplies a and b to produce p and q, respectively, p:q = a:b by 7.17. Since a and b multiply b to produce q and r, respectively, q:r = a:b by 7.18. These are the directly applicable forms: 7.17 concerns a common multiplier, and 7.18 a common number multiplied. [7.17, 7.18]

**Step 3.** Since a multiplies p and q to produce C and M, respectively, C:M = p:q. Likewise, since a multiplies q and r to produce M and N, respectively, M:N = q:r. Combining these proportions with Step 2 gives C:M = a:b and M:N = a:b. [7.17, 5.11]

**Step 4.** Since a and b multiply r to produce N and D, respectively, N:D = a:b. Consequently,
C:M = M:N = N:D = a:b.
Thus C, M, N, D are in continued proportion, and M and N are the two mean proportional numbers between the given cubes. [7.18, 5.11]

**Step 5.** For four continuously proportional numbers, the first has to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Hence C:D is triplicate of C:M; and C:M = a:b by Step 3. Therefore the cube C has to the cube D the ratio triplicate of that which its side a has to the side b, as required. [D5.10]

**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and each by multiplying itself make some number, the products will be proportional; and, if the original numbers by multiplying the products make certain numbers, the latter will also be proportional.

**Step 2.** Take any three consecutive original numbers aᵢ, aᵢ₊₁, aᵢ₊₂. By hypothesis, aᵢ:aᵢ₊₁ = aᵢ₊₁:aᵢ₊₂. By 8.11 and the definition of duplicate ratio, there are mean proportional numbers p and q such that
Sᵢ:p = p:Sᵢ₊₁ = aᵢ:aᵢ₊₁,
and
Sᵢ₊₁:q = q:Sᵢ₊₂ = aᵢ₊₁:aᵢ₊₂. [8.11, D5.9]

**Step 3.** Consequently, the chains Sᵢ, p, Sᵢ₊₁ and Sᵢ₊₁, q, Sᵢ₊₂ have equal corresponding successive ratios. [5.11] Therefore, ex aequali,
Sᵢ:Sᵢ₊₁ = Sᵢ₊₁:Sᵢ₊₂. [7.14]

**Step 4.** Likewise, by 8.12 and the definition of triplicate ratio, there are intermediate numbers u, v and w, x such that
Tᵢ:u = u:v = v:Tᵢ₊₁ = aᵢ:aᵢ₊₁,
and
Tᵢ₊₁:w = w:x = x:Tᵢ₊₂ = aᵢ₊₁:aᵢ₊₂. [8.12, D5.10]

**Step 5.** Since aᵢ:aᵢ₊₁ = aᵢ₊₁:aᵢ₊₂, these two four-term chains also have equal corresponding successive ratios. [5.11] Hence, ex aequali,
Tᵢ:Tᵢ₊₁ = Tᵢ₊₁:Tᵢ₊₂. [7.14]

**Step 6.** The three consecutive original numbers were arbitrary. Thus every consecutive triple of the Sᵢ is proportional, and every consecutive triple of the Tᵢ is proportional. ## Proposition 8.14
**Statement:** If a square measure a square, the side will also measure the side; and, if the side measure the side, the square will also measure the square.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be square numbers with sides a and b respectively, so that A = a·a and B = b·b (D7.18). Form M = a·b (D7.15).

**Step 2.** Since a multiplies a and b to produce A and M, respectively, A:M = a:b (7.17). Since a and b multiply b to produce M and B, respectively, M:B = a:b (7.18). Thus A, M, B are in continued proportion, and both successive ratios equal a:b. ## Proposition 8.15
**Statement:** If a cube number measure a cube number, the side will also measure the side; and, if the side measure the side, the cube will also measure the cube.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be cube numbers with sides a and b. Put p = a·a, q = a·b, and r = b·b. Thus A = a·p and B = b·r. Form also M = a·q and N = b·q. These products are defined by multiplication, and A and B are the corresponding cubes. [D7.15, D7.19]

**Step 2.** Since a multiplies a and b to produce p and q, we have p:q = a:b. Since a multiplies p and q to produce A and M, we have A:M = p:q. [7.17] Since a and b multiply b to produce q and r, and multiply q to produce M and N, we have q:r = a:b and M:N = a:b. [7.18] Finally, since b multiplies q and r to produce N and B, we have N:B = q:r. [7.17] Consequently,
A:M = M:N = N:B = a:b.
Thus A, M, N, B are in continued proportion.

**Step 3.** Suppose first that A measures B. Then A measures M by 8.7. This is the direct path: the hypothesis concerns the extreme terms of the continued proportion, so the extremes-to-second assertion applies immediately. [8.7]

**Step 4.** Since A:M = a:b, a is the same part of b that A is of M. Hence a measures b. Thus, if the cube measures the cube, its side measures the other side. [D7.20, D7.3]

**Step 5.** Conversely, suppose that a measures b, and let b consist of k copies of a. From A:M = M:N = N:B = a:b, each antecedent is the same part of its consequent that a is of b. Therefore M consists of k copies of A, N of k copies of M, and B of k copies of N. [D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 6.** Expanding these repeated sums, B consists of k·k·k copies of A. Hence A measures B. Therefore, if a cube number measures a cube number, its side measures the other side; and, if the side measures the side, the cube measures the cube. [D7.15, D7.3]

## Proposition 8.16
**Statement:** If a square number do not measure a square number, neither will the side measure the side; and, if the side do not measure the side, neither will the square measure the square.

## Proposition 8.21
**Statement:** If two mean proportional numbers fall between two numbers, the numbers are similar solid numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the given numbers, and let M and N be their two mean proportionals. Thus
A:M = M:N = N:B.
We must show that A and B have representations as solid numbers with proportional corresponding sides. [D7.20, D7.21]

**Step 2.** Choose the least terms E and F having the ratio A:B. Such terms can be found by 7.33, and they are prime to one another by 7.22. Our path is to reduce the endpoint ratio: this supplies precisely the coprimality needed to pass from the given means to means adjoining the unit. [7.33, 7.22]

**Step 3.** Since A:B = E:F, the two mean proportionals between A and B imply that two mean proportionals also fall between E and F. Since E and F are prime to one another, two mean proportionals therefore fall between each of them and the unit. [8.8, 8.9]

**Step 4.** Write these latter progressions as
E:U = U:r = r:1,
and
F:V = V:s = s:1.
The first progression gives U = r·r and E = r·U = r·r·r; the second gives V = s·s and F = s·V = s·s·s. These equalities follow directly from the definition of numerical proportion and multiplication. Thus E and F are cubes. If a least term is itself the unit, its corresponding expression is simply 1 = 1·1·1. [D7.20, D7.15, D7.19]

**Step 5.** The least terms E and F measure A and B respectively the same number of times. Denote this common multiplicity by k, allowing k to be the unit when the pairs coincide. Hence
A = kE = (kr)·r·r,
and
B = kF = (ks)·s·s.
The regrouping follows from multiplication as repeated addition. Accordingly, these are solid representations of A and B, with sides kr, r, r and ks, s, s respectively. [7.20, D7.15, D7.17]

**Step 6.** Multiplication by the same number preserves the ratio, so kr:ks = r:s; when k is the unit this equality is immediate. Therefore the three corresponding side-ratios are equal:
kr:ks = r:s = r:s.
The solid numbers A and B consequently have their sides proportional, and hence are similar solid numbers, as required. [7.17, D7.21]

## Proposition 8.22
**Statement:** If three numbers be in continued proportion, and the first be square, the third will also be square.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be in continued proportion, so that A:B = B:C, and let A be square. Take its side s, so that A = s·s. (Hypothesis; D7.18.)

**Step 3.** Apply 8.14: since the square A measures the square B·B, its side s measures the side B. This is the direct square-divisibility route, chosen because the required divisibility has just been established. Write B = s·t. The multiplier t is a number, not merely the unit: otherwise B = s and B·B = A, whereas Step 2 gives B·B = A·C > A, since C is a multitude of units. (8.14; D7.3; D7.15; D7.2; CN5.)

**Step 4.** Multiplication of s and t by s produces A and B respectively. Hence A:B = s:t. (7.17.)

**Step 5.** Let T = t·t, which is square by D7.18. Since t·s = s·t = B by 7.16, multiplication of s and t by t produces B and T respectively. Thus B:T = s:t. (7.17.)

**Step 6.** Steps 4 and 5 give A:B = B:T by 5.11. Together with the given proportion A:B = B:C, this yields B:C = B:T, again by 5.11. Therefore C = T by 5.9. Since T = t·t, C is square, as required. (D7.18.)

## Proposition 8.23
**Statement:** If four numbers be in continued proportion, and the first be cube, the fourth will also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be in continued proportion, so that A:B = B:C = C:D, and suppose A is a cube. Let a be its side, so A = a³. Put s = a²; then A² = a⁶ = s³, by regrouping repeated multiplication. [D7.19, D7.15]

**Step 2.** From A:B = B:C, the products of the extremes and means are equal, giving AC = B². Likewise, from A:B = C:D, we obtain AD = BC. [7.19]

**Step 3.** Multiplying the first equality by B and using the second, we obtain
B³ = B(AC) = A(BC) = A(AD) = A²D = s³D.
Here multiplying equal numbers preserves equality by repeated addition, and the products may be regrouped and their factors interchanged. [D7.15, CN2, 7.16]

**Step 4.** Thus the cube s³ measures the cube B³. Consequently s measures B. We use the forward cube-divisibility implication of 8.15 because Step 3 supplies exactly its hypothesis. Write B = st, where t is the integral multiplier, possibly initially a unit. [D7.5, 8.15, D7.15]

**Step 5.** Cubing B = st gives B³ = s³t³, by regrouping and interchanging the factors. Together with Step 3, this yields
s³D = s³t³.
[D7.15, 7.16, CN1]

**Step 6.** Therefore D = t³. Indeed, if D and t³ were unequal, adding the greater to itself s³ times would give a greater result than adding the lesser to itself equally many times: the former sum would contain the latter together with a positive excess. This contradicts Step 5. [D7.15, CN2, CN5] Since D is a number, t cannot be merely a unit. Hence D is the product of three equal numbers t, and is therefore a cube, as required. [D7.2, D7.19]

## Proposition 9.1
**Statement:** If two similar plane numbers by multiplying one another make some number, the product will be square.

**Step 4.** Therefore P is produced by multiplying the number M by itself, and hence is square by D7.18. Thus the product of two similar plane numbers is square.

## Proposition 9.4
**Statement:** If a cube number by multiplying a cube number make some number, the product will be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be cube numbers, and let C be the product obtained when A multiplies B. Let D be the product obtained when A multiplies itself. Since A is a cube, D is a cube by **9.3**. Our path is to compare C with this known cube D.

**Step 2.** The same number A, multiplying A and B respectively, produces D and C. Therefore the products have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied:
D : C = A : B. (**7.17**)

**Step 3.** Thus D and C have to one another the ratio of the cube A to the cube B. By **8.25**, if two numbers have the ratio of a cube to a cube and the first is a cube, the second is also a cube. This ratio criterion applies directly to the proportion in Step 2. Since D is a cube by Step 1, C is a cube. Therefore a cube number multiplied by a cube number produces a cube.

## Proposition 9.5
**Statement:** If a cube number by multiplying any number make a cube number, the multiplied number will also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let the cube number A multiply the number B to produce the cube number C, so AB=C (D7.15). Let a and c be their respective sides: A=(a·a)·a and C=(c·c)·c (D7.19).

**Step 2.** Since AB=C, A measures C (D7.15). Therefore a measures c, by 8.15. This is the direct path: the hypothesis already supplies measurement between cubes, and 8.15 immediately transfers that measurement to their sides.

**Step 3.** Let d be the number of times a measures c; thus c=ad (D7.15). This measure-count is not merely a unit. For then c=a and consequently C=A, whereas AB=C is greater than A: B is a multitude of units, so AB contains A together with further copies of A (D7.2, D7.15, CN5). Hence d is a number.

**Step 4.** Form D=(d·d)·d, which is a cube number (D7.19). Regrouping multiplication by expanding it as repeated addition (D7.15), and interchanging factors by 7.16, gives
AD=((a·a)·a)((d·d)·d)=((ad)·(ad))·(ad)=(c·c)·c=C.

**Step 5.** Since AB=C and AD=C, AB=AD (CN1). Therefore B=D. Indeed, if either B or D were greater, multiplying it by A would give a greater product: by D7.15 and 7.16, that product would contain all the copies of A in the other product and additional copies, contrary to equality (CN5). Since D is a cube, B is a cube also (D7.19). Thus the multiplied number is cube.

## Proposition 9.6
**Statement:** If a number by multiplying itself make a cube number, it will itself also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given number, and let B be the number produced by multiplying A by itself, so B = A·A. By hypothesis, B is a cube. [D7.15; hypothesis]

**Step 2.** Let B by multiplying A produce C. Then C = (A·A)·A, so C is contained by three equal numbers A, A, A. Therefore C is a cube. [D7.15; D7.19]

**Step 3.** Thus the cube B, by multiplying A, makes the cube C. Apply 9.5 directly, since both its cube hypotheses have now been established: the multiplied number A is itself a cube, as required. [9.5]

## Proposition 9.7
**Statement:** If a composite number by multiplying any number make some number, the product will be solid.

**Step 1.** Let the composite number A multiply any number B to produce C. Since A is composite, choose a proper numerical measure D of A. We take the direct definitional route, using this measure to exhibit three numbers producing C. [D7.13]

**Step 2.** Let E be the multitude of times D measures A. Since D is less than A, this multitude contains more than one unit, so E is a number. Thus A consists of D added to itself as many times as there are units in E; that is, E multiplying D produces A. [D7.2, D7.15]

**Step 3.** Therefore E multiplying D produces A, and this resulting number A multiplying B produces C by hypothesis. Hence the three numbers E, D, and B, multiplied successively, produce C. By the definition of a solid number, C is solid, as required. [D7.17]

## Proposition 9.8
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the third from the unit will be square, as will also those which successively leave out one; the fourth will be cube, as will also all those which leave out two; and the seventh will be at once cube and square, as will also those which leave out five.

**Step 1.** Let the given progression be u₀, u₁, …, u_N, where u₀ = 1 is the unit, and put a = u₁. Count the unit as the first term. By hypothesis, u_j : u_{j+1} = 1 : a. Since a consists of units, u_{j+1} therefore consists of as many copies of u_j as there are units in a. Consequently, for every j ≥ 1 for which the next term occurs,
u_{j+1} = a·u_j.
Here x·y denotes the product obtained when x multiplies y. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 2.** Path choice: use 7.18, since we shall keep the multiplied number fixed while the multipliers run through the progression. Fix positive indices r and s with r+s ≤ N, and form P_j = u_j·u_r for j = 1, …, s. For each adjacent pair, multiplication of the same number u_r gives
P_j : P_{j+1} = u_j : u_{j+1}.
Thus P_{j+1}, like u_{j+1} relative to u_j, consists of as many copies of P_j as there are units in a; that is, P_{j+1} = a·P_j. [7.18, D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 3.** The first product is P₁ = a·u_r = u_{r+1}, by Step 1. Whenever P_j = u_{r+j}, adding the same number of copies of these equal numbers gives P_{j+1} = u_{r+j+1}, by Steps 1–2 and CN2. Repeating this along the finite sequence proves P_s = u_{r+s}. Hence, whenever r and s are positive and the indicated term occurs,
u_{r+s} = u_s·u_r. [D7.15, CN2]

**Step 4.** Taking s = r in Step 3 gives u_{2r} = u_r·u_r. Therefore every such u_{2r} is square, being equal multiplied by equal. Its position, counting the unit first, is 2r+1. These are precisely the third, fifth, seventh, and successive terms obtained by leaving out one term each time. [Step 3; D7.18]

**Step 5.** Taking s = 2r in Step 3 gives u_{3r} = u_{2r}·u_r. By Step 4, u_{2r} = u_r·u_r; hence
u_{3r} = (u_r·u_r)·u_r.
Thus u_{3r} is cube, being equal multiplied by equal and again by equal. Its position is 3r+1: the fourth, seventh, tenth, and successive terms obtained by leaving out two terms each time. [Steps 3–4; D7.19]

**Step 6.** Whenever u_{6r} occurs, Step 4 applied with index 3r shows that it is square, while Step 5 applied with index 2r shows that it is cube. Its position is 6r+1: the seventh, thirteenth, nineteenth, and successive terms obtained by leaving out five terms each time. Thus all three assertions hold throughout the given progression. [Steps 4–5; D7.18, D7.19]

## Proposition 9.9
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be square, all the rest will also be square.

**Step 1.** Let u, A_1, A_2, …, A_n be in continued proportion, where u is the unit and A_1 is square. Thus, for each i with 1 ≤ i < n, u : A_1 = A_i : A_{i+1}. [Hypothesis; D7.20]

**Step 2.** The unit measures A_1 as many times as there are units in A_1. By the proportion in Step 1, A_i measures A_{i+1} the same number of times. Hence A_{i+1} consists of A_i added to itself as many times as there are units in A_1: it is precisely the number produced when A_1 multiplies A_i. [D7.2, D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 3.** Suppose A_i is square. Since A_1 is also square, there are numbers r and s such that A_1 is produced by r multiplying r, and A_i by s multiplying s. These are plane numbers with sides r, r and s, s respectively. Since r : r = s : s, their sides are proportional; therefore A_1 and A_i are similar plane numbers. [D7.18, D7.16, D7.20, D7.21]

**Step 4.** Apply 9.1: two similar plane numbers, by multiplying one another, produce a square. Therefore the product of A_1 and A_i, which is A_{i+1} by Step 2, is square. This is the direct path: the similar-plane representation of the two squares makes the product criterion immediately applicable. [9.1; Steps 2–3]

**Step 5.** Starting with the given square A_1, Step 4 proves successively that A_2 is square, then A_3, and so on through A_n. Thus all the remaining numbers in the continued proportion are square, as required. [Hypothesis; Steps 3–4]

## Proposition 9.10
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be not square, neither will any other be square except the third from the unit and all those which leave out one.

**Step 1.** Write the given progression as u, A₁, A₂, …, Aₘ, where u is the unit and A₁ is not square. Its consecutive ratios are equal by hypothesis (D7.20). Counting the unit as the first term, the third term and those which successively leave out one are A₂, A₄, A₆, … .

**Step 2.** By 9.8, every such term A₂, A₄, A₆, … that occurs in the progression is square. It therefore remains to exclude squares among the odd-indexed terms.

**Step 3.** Suppose, for a contradiction, that some later odd-indexed term A₂ₖ₊₁ is square, where k ≥ 1. Consider the two lists
A₁, A₂, …, Aₖ₊₁
and
Aₖ₊₁, Aₖ₊₂, …, A₂ₖ₊₁.
They contain equally many terms, and corresponding consecutive ratios are equal. Hence, by 7.14,
A₁ : Aₖ₊₁ = Aₖ₊₁ : A₂ₖ₊₁.

**Step 4.** Inverting this proportion gives
A₂ₖ₊₁ : Aₖ₊₁ = Aₖ₊₁ : A₁
(D7.20). Thus these three numbers, in reverse order, are in continued proportion. The direct three-term route is appropriate here: 8.22 states that if three numbers are in continued proportion and the first is square, the third is also square. Since A₂ₖ₊₁ was supposed square, 8.22 makes A₁ square, contrary to the hypothesis.

**Step 5.** Consequently no later odd-indexed term is square, and A₁ itself is not square by hypothesis. Together with Step 2, this proves that the only square numbers in the progression are the third term from the unit and all those which successively leave out one, as required.

## Proposition 9.11
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the less measures the greater according to some one of the numbers which have place among the proportional numbers.

**Step 1.** Let a₀, a₁, …, aₙ be the given continued proportion, where a₀ is the unit. Thus a₀:a₁ = aₖ:aₖ₊₁ for every k < n. Since a₁ contains more than one unit, each aₖ₊₁ consists of as many copies of aₖ as a₁ contains units (D7.1, D7.2, D7.20). Consequently aₖ₊₁ > aₖ, so the terms increase in their given order (CN5).

**Step 2.** Choose any less term aᵢ and greater term aⱼ. By Step 1, i < j. Put d = j − i, and consider the two chains
(a₀, a₁, …, a_d) and (aᵢ, aᵢ₊₁, …, aⱼ).
They contain equally many terms, and every consecutive ratio in either chain equals the common ratio of the given continued proportion (hypothesis; D7.20).

**Step 3.** The direct path is numerical ex aequali: it applies immediately to these equal-length chains with matching consecutive ratios. Hence their extreme terms are proportional:
a₀:a_d = aᵢ:aⱼ (7.14).

**Step 4.** The unit a₀ measures a_d as many times as there are units in a_d (D7.1, D7.2). By the proportion in Step 3, aᵢ is the same part of aⱼ that a₀ is of a_d (D7.20). Therefore aᵢ measures aⱼ that same number of times—that is, according to a_d (D7.3). Since 1 ≤ d ≤ n, a_d is one of the numbers in the given continued proportion. Thus the less measures the greater according to some one of the numbers having place among the proportional numbers.

## Proposition 9.12
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same.

**Step 1.** Let u, a₁, a₂, …, aₙ be the given finite sequence beginning with the unit u and continuing in proportion. Let p be any prime number measuring aₙ. We must show that p measures a₁. If n = 1, this is already the hypothesis; therefore suppose n ≥ 2. [Hypothesis]

**Step 2.** For each j from 2 through n, continued proportion gives u : a₁ = aⱼ₋₁ : aⱼ. The unit measures a₁ as many times as there are units in a₁; hence aⱼ₋₁ measures aⱼ that same number of times. Thus a₁ multiplied by aⱼ₋₁ produces aⱼ:
 aⱼ = a₁ · aⱼ₋₁. [D7.2, D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 3.** The direct path is to apply the prime-divisor-of-a-product proposition, since Step 2 supplies exactly such products. Whenever p measures aⱼ with j ≥ 2, it measures at least one of the factors a₁ and aⱼ₋₁. [7.30; Step 2]

**Step 4.** Begin with p measuring aₙ. By Step 3, either p measures a₁, as required, or it measures aₙ₋₁. In the latter case apply Step 3 again, continuing backwards through the finite sequence unless p has already been shown to measure a₁. If a₂ is reached, then a₂ = a₁ · a₁, so p necessarily measures a₁. Thus every prime number measuring the last term also measures the term next to the unit. Consequently, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit is measured by those same primes. [7.30; Steps 1–3]

## Proposition 9.13
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be prime, the greatest will not be measured by any except those which have a place among the proportional numbers.

**Step 1.** Let the given continued proportion be
\[a_0=1,\quad a_1=p,\quad a_2,\ldots,a_n,\]
where 1 is the unit and p is prime. Since \(1:p=a_i:a_{i+1}\), each \(a_{i+1}\) consists of p copies of \(a_i\). Because p is a number, it exceeds the unit; consequently the terms increase strictly, and \(a_n\) is the greatest. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.20, D7.15, CN5]

**Step 2.** Suppose that a number d measures \(a_n\) but equals none of the listed terms. Then \(d<a_n\). Among the listed terms that measure d, choose the one with greatest index, say \(a_k\). Such a term exists because the unit measures every number. Since d is not a listed term, \(a_k<d<a_n\); hence \(k<n\), and \(a_{k+1}\) exists. Our path is to show that this next term also measures d, contradicting the choice of k. [D7.2, D7.3, CN5]

**Step 3.** Let q be the number of times \(a_k\) measures d, so that d consists of q copies of \(a_k\). Since \(a_k<d\), q exceeds the unit. Moreover, q measures d: if \(a_k\) is the unit, then \(q=d\); otherwise, interchange the factors by 7.16, so that d also consists of \(a_k\) copies of q. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.15, 7.16]

**Step 4.** By 7.32, q either is prime or has a prime measure; thus choose a prime r equal to q or measuring q. This proposition is appropriate because q has not been assumed composite. Since q measures d and d measures \(a_n\), r measures \(a_n\): replacing each successive measure by its constituent copies gives copies of r. By 9.12, r therefore measures the term p immediately after the unit. Since p is prime and r is a number, \(r=p\). Consequently q either equals p or is measured by p. [7.32, D7.15, 9.12, D7.11]

**Step 5.** Group the q copies of \(a_k\) constituting d into groups of p copies. This is possible by Step 4. Each group equals \(a_{k+1}\), by Step 1, so \(a_{k+1}\) measures d. This contradicts the maximal choice of k in Step 2. Hence no number outside the given progression measures \(a_n\). The unit is already its first term, so the greatest is measured only by terms having a place in the given continued proportion. [D7.15; Steps 1–4]

## Proposition 9.14
**Statement:** If a number be the least that is measured by prime numbers, it will not be measured by any other prime number except those originally measuring it.

**Step 1.** Let N be the least number measured by the given prime numbers p₁, …, pᵣ. Suppose, for contradiction, that another prime q measures N, with q different from every pᵢ. [Hypothesis; D7.11.]

**Step 2.** None of the pᵢ measures q, since q is prime and each pᵢ is a number different from q. Consequently N cannot equal q, because every pᵢ measures N. [D7.11; Step 1.]

**Step 3.** Since q measures N, let M be the number of times it measures N. Thus M multiplying q produces N. Because N is not q, M is a number rather than the unit. Moreover, taking one unit from each of these M copies of q gives M units and leaves units over, since q is itself a number. Hence M is less than N. [D7.5; D7.15; D7.2; CN5; Step 2.]

**Step 4.** Take any of the given primes pᵢ. It measures N, the product of M and q; therefore it measures M or q, by 7.30. It does not measure q by Step 2, so it measures M. Thus every given prime measures M. The direct path is to use 7.30 here, because the required product is already supplied by the supposed extra prime divisor. [7.30; Steps 1–3.]

**Step 5.** Therefore M is a number less than N measured by all the given primes, contradicting the hypothesis that N is the least such number. Hence no prime other than the originally given primes measures N. [Steps 3–4; leastness hypothesis.]

## Proposition 9.15
**Statement:** If three numbers in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, any two whatever added together will be prime to the remaining number.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the given numbers, least among those having their ratio, with A:B = B:C. By 8.3, A and C are prime to one another. By 7.19, AC = B², where B² denotes B multiplied by itself. **Path choice:** 8.3 applies immediately to the leastness hypothesis; the product identity then permits a direct argument using prime measures.

**Step 2.** If two numbers are not prime to one another, they have a common numerical measure d (D7.12). By 7.32, d either is prime or is measured by a prime; consequently, the two numbers have a prime common measure p (D7.5, D7.15). We use 7.32 because d is arbitrary, not assumed composite. We shall also use these elementary consequences of measurement: a measure of either factor measures their product (D7.15, 7.16), and a common measure of a whole and a part measures the remainder, since removing whole copies of the measure leaves whole copies (D7.5, CN3).

**Step 3.** Suppose A+B and C are not prime to one another. By Step 2, some prime p measures both. Since p measures C, it measures AC, hence B² by Step 1 (D7.15, 7.16). Therefore p measures B, by 7.30 applied to B multiplied by itself. Since p measures A+B and B, it also measures A (D7.5, CN3). Thus p measures both A and C, contradicting their being prime to one another (Step 1; D7.12). Hence A+B is prime to C.

**Step 4.** Suppose B+C and A are not prime to one another. By Step 2, some prime p measures both. Since p measures A, it measures AC = B² (D7.15, 7.16; Step 1). By 7.30, p therefore measures B. Subtracting B from B+C shows that p also measures C (D7.5, CN3). Again p measures both A and C, contradicting Step 1 and D7.12. Hence B+C is prime to A.

**Step 5.** Suppose A+C and B are not prime to one another. By Step 2, some prime p measures both. Since p measures B, it measures B² = AC (D7.15; Step 1). By 7.30, p measures A or C. If it measures A, subtracting A from A+C shows that it measures C; if it measures C, subtracting C shows that it measures A (D7.5, CN3). Either way, p measures both extremes, contradicting Step 1 and D7.12. Hence A+C is prime to B.

**Step 6.** Steps 3–5 establish all three possible choices. Therefore any two of the given numbers added together are prime to the remaining number, as required.

## Proposition 9.16
**Statement:** If two numbers be prime to one another, the second will not be to any other number as the first is to the second.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be numbers prime to one another. Thus their only common measure is an unit [D7.12]. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is a number C such that A:B = B:C.

**Step 2.** Since A and B are prime to one another, they are the least numbers having their ratio [7.21]. We choose the least-terms route because 7.21 applies directly to the given coprimality.

**Step 3.** The least numbers having a given ratio measure the corresponding numbers of any pair having that ratio [7.20]. Applying this to A:B = B:C, we obtain that A measures B.

**Step 4.** Since A also measures itself once, A is a common measure of A and B. But A is a number, a multitude of units, and not an unit [D7.1, D7.2]. This contradicts their being prime to one another [D7.12]. Therefore no number C can satisfy B:C = A:B: the second cannot be to any other number as the first is to the second.

## Proposition 9.17
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the extremes of them be prime to one another, the last will not be to any other number as the first to the second.

**Step 1.** Let A_1, A_2, …, A_n be numbers in continued proportion, with A_1 and A_n prime to one another. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is a number B such that A_n : B = A_1 : A_2. Then A_1, A_2, …, A_n, B are in continued proportion, since the appended ratio equals their common ratio (hypothesis; D7.20).

**Step 2.** Path choice: apply the numerical ex aequali theorem to the original sequence and its one-place shift; this directly brings the given coprime extremes into a proportion. The two sequences
A_1, A_2, …, A_n
and
A_2, A_3, …, A_n, B
have corresponding successive ratios equal. Therefore, ex aequali,
A_1 : A_n = A_2 : B (7.14).

**Step 3.** Since A_1 and A_n are prime to one another, they are the least numbers having their ratio (7.21). The least numbers having a given ratio measure the corresponding numbers of any pair having that ratio (7.20). Applying this to the proportion in Step 2, we conclude that A_1 measures A_2.

**Step 4.** Because all successive ratios in the original sequence are equal, each succeeding term consists of the same whole number of copies of its predecessor as A_2 does of A_1 (D7.20). Thus A_2 consists of copies of A_1, A_3 consists of copies of A_2, and so on. Repeatedly substituting these decompositions expresses A_n as a whole number of copies of A_1; hence A_1 measures A_n (D7.15).

**Step 5.** Consequently, A_1 itself measures both A_1 and A_n. Since A_1 is a number, and therefore a multitude of units rather than an unit, this contradicts the hypothesis that their only common measure is an unit (D7.2; D7.12). ## Proposition 9.18
**Statement:** Given two numbers, to investigate whether it is possible to find a third proportional to them.

**Step 1.** Let the given numbers, in their assigned order, be A and B. Form S = B·B by repeated addition [D7.15, D7.18]. By 7.19, a number C satisfies A:B = B:C if and only if A·C = S. **Path choice:** use this product criterion directly, rather than first reducing the ratio to least terms, because it immediately supplies a measurement test [7.19].

**Step 2.** Starting with S, repeatedly subtract A while possible, counting the copies removed. Stop when nothing remains or when the remainder is smaller than A. This process terminates: S consists of finitely many units, and each subtraction removes units and leaves a strictly smaller remainder [D7.2, CN5].

**Step 3.** Suppose S is exhausted after at least two copies of A have been removed. Let C be the number containing as many units as there were copies removed [D7.2]. Then A·C = S by the definition of multiplication [D7.15]. Since S = B·B, proposition 7.19 gives A:B = B:C. Thus C is the required third proportional [7.19].

**Step 4.** Suppose instead that a nonempty remainder is left, or that S is exhausted after only one copy of A. If a third proportional number C existed, 7.19 would give S = A·C. By the definition of multiplication, S would therefore consist of exactly as many copies of A as there are units in C [D7.15]. Since C is a number, not merely a unit, the subtraction would exhaust S after at least two copies, contrary to the outcome of the test [D7.1, D7.2]. Hence no third proportional number exists in these cases. Consequently, a third proportional exists exactly when B·B consists of whole copies of A whose count is a number rather than a single unit; the finite test above both decides the question and constructs the third proportional whenever possible [7.19, D7.15].

## Proposition 9.19
**Statement:** Given three numbers, to investigate when it is possible to find a fourth proportional to them.

**Step 1.** Let the three given numbers, in their prescribed order, be A, B, C. We seek a number X such that A:B = C:X (D7.20). **Path choice:** use 7.19 directly, since it characterizes this four-term proportion by equality of products and avoids first reducing A:B to least terms.

**Step 2.** Form the product P = BC (D7.15). From P repeatedly subtract A whenever the remainder contains at least A units, recording one unit for each subtraction. This process terminates: P consists of finitely many units, and each subtraction removes a positive multitude of them (D7.1, D7.2). Thus we can determine whether the subtraction exhausts P exactly and, if so, how many copies of A it contained.

**Step 3.** Suppose the process exhausts P exactly and the recorded units constitute a number X. Then X copies of A make P, so XA = P by D7.15. By 7.16, AX = XA; hence AX = BC (CN1). Therefore A:B = C:X by the converse direction of 7.19. The required fourth proportional has been constructed.

**Step 4.** Conversely, suppose a fourth proportional number Y exists, so that A:B = C:Y. By 7.19, AY = BC = P; and by 7.16, YA = P. Consequently P consists of exactly Y copies of A (D7.15). The procedure in Step 2 must therefore exhaust P exactly, recording the number Y. Thus, if that procedure leaves a remainder, or does not record a number of copies, no fourth proportional number exists.

**Step 5.** The investigation is therefore complete: multiply the second given number by the third, and test by repeated subtraction whether the product contains the first an exact number of times. If it does, that number of times is the fourth proportional; otherwise none exists, by Steps 3–4 and 7.19. In particular, if BC = A, the procedure records only an unit, not a number in Euclid’s terminology, so this boundary case supplies an unit rather than a fourth proportional number (D7.1, D7.2).

## Proposition 9.20
**Statement:** Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.

**Step 1.** Let p₁, …, pᵣ be any assigned finite collection of distinct prime numbers. Construct a common multiple M as follows: begin with p₁, and successively take the least common multiple of the current number and the next assigned prime by 7.34. Every earlier prime continues to measure the resulting number, since repeating a sum of copies of that prime again gives a sum of copies of it [D7.15]. Thus every pᵢ measures M. If only one prime is assigned, take M = p₁. Construction choice: only the common-multiple property is needed; leastness is not used.

**Step 2.** Let u be a unit and form N = M + u, which is a number [D7.1, D7.2]. Since each pᵢ measures M, each is at most M; and N is greater than M. Consequently N is greater than every assigned prime [D7.5, CN5].

**Step 3.** By 7.32, N either is prime or is measured by some prime number. This unconditional alternative is the direct choice because the primality of N has not been determined. If N is prime, Step 2 already gives a prime different from all the assigned primes. In the other case, let q be a prime measuring N [7.32].

**Step 4.** Suppose that q were one of the assigned primes. Then q would measure M by Step 1, as well as N by Step 3. Express M and N as sums of copies of q. Since N > M, cancelling from the latter sum the copies that make M leaves a positive number of copies of q equal to N − M = u [D7.15, CN3].

**Step 5.** But q, being a number, is a multitude of units and is therefore greater than a single unit [D7.1, D7.2, CN5]. A positive sum of copies of q cannot equal u: one copy already exceeds u, and further copies only increase the whole [CN5]. Thus the supposition in Step 4 is impossible, and q is different from every assigned prime.

**Step 6.** In either alternative of Step 3, a prime has been found outside the assigned collection. Adjoining it produces a collection of prime numbers greater in multitude than the assigned collection, which is a proper part of the enlarged collection [Steps 3–5, CN5]. Since the assigned collection was arbitrary, prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.

## Proposition 9.21
**Statement:** If as many even numbers as we please be added together, the whole is even.

**Step 1.** We proceed directly from the definition of evenness, which supplies the required equal parts. Let A₁, …, Aₙ be any finite collection of even numbers. Divide each Aᵢ into two parts Bᵢ and Cᵢ such that Bᵢ = Cᵢ. [D7.6]

**Step 3.** These two totals together contain exactly the two parts of every original summand, so they constitute the whole A₁ + ⋯ + Aₙ. By Steps 1–2, the whole is therefore divided into two equal parts, B and C. Hence the whole is even. [D7.6]

## Proposition 9.23
**Statement:** If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be odd, the whole will also be odd.

**Step 1.** Let an odd multitude of odd numbers be given. If there is only one summand, their sum is odd by hypothesis. Otherwise, set aside one summand A. Since the original multitude is odd, the remaining multitude is even. [D7.7]

**Step 3.** Remove one unit from A, and call the remainder B. Since A is odd, B is even, and A = B + 1. [D7.7]

**Step 4.** Since E and B are both even, E + B is even. Adding E to the equality A = B + 1 shows that the sum S of all the given numbers satisfies S = E + A = (E + B) + 1. [9.21; CN2]

**Step 5.** Thus S exceeds the even number E + B by one unit, so S is odd. Therefore, if an odd multitude of odd numbers is added together, the whole is odd. [D7.7]

## Proposition 9.24
**Statement:** If from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be even.

**Step 1.** Let A be an even number, B a smaller even number, and R the remainder after subtracting B from A. We use the defining division into equal parts directly: write A = A₁ + A₂ and B = B₁ + B₂, where A₁ = A₂ and B₁ = B₂. (D7.6)

Both alternatives contradict A > B. (CN2, CN5)

**Step 3.** Subtract B₁ from A₁ and B₂ from A₂, calling the remainders C₁ and C₂. Since A₁ = A₂ and B₁ = B₂, the remainders are equal: C₁ = C₂. (CN3)

**Step 4.** Combining A₁ = B₁ + C₁ and A₂ = B₂ + C₂ gives A = B + (C₁ + C₂). Subtracting B therefore gives R = C₁ + C₂. (CN2, CN3)

**Step 5.** Thus R is divided into the two equal parts C₁ and C₂. Therefore R is even: subtracting an even number from an even number leaves an even remainder. (D7.6)

**Statement:** If an odd number measure an even number, it will also measure the half of it.

## Proposition 9.32
**Statement:** Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.

**Step 1.** Let u be the unit and A₀ the dyad, u + u. Let A₁, A₂, …, Aᵣ be its successive doubles, so that Aᵢ = Aᵢ₋₁ + Aᵢ₋₁. Here A₀ is the starting dyad, and A₁, …, Aᵣ are the numbers obtained by doubling it. The dyad is even because it consists of two equal units; every subsequent term is even because it consists of two equal parts. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.6]

**Step 2.** Choose any of these doubled numbers, N = Aₖ, where k ≥ 1. Its predecessor Aₖ₋₁ measures N according to the dyad, since two copies of Aₖ₋₁ make N. Both the predecessor and the dyad are even by Step 1. Therefore N is even-times even. [D7.15, D7.8]

**Step 3.** To establish exclusivity, use descent by halves: proposition 9.30 applies directly to the given doubling chain. Suppose an odd number O measures N. Since N is even, O also measures its half Aₖ₋₁. Repeating 9.30 along the chain shows that O measures A₀, the dyad. Applying 9.30 once more shows that O measures its half, the unit. This is impossible: a number is a multitude of units and therefore exceeds a single unit, whereas even one copy of it cannot be contained in the unit. Thus no odd number measures N. [9.30, D7.1, D7.2, CN5]

**Step 4.** Suppose N were also even-times odd. Then an even number E would measure N according to an odd number O; that is, O multiplying E would produce N. By commutativity of multiplication, E multiplying O would also produce N, so O would measure N. This contradicts Step 3. Hence N is not even-times odd. [D7.9, D7.15, 7.16]

**Step 5.** Thus N is even-times even, but not even-times odd: it is even-times even only. Since N was any number obtained by successive doubling from the dyad, each of the stated numbers is even-times even only. [D7.8, D7.9]

## Proposition 9.34
**Statement:** If a number neither be one of those which are continually doubled from a dyad, nor have its half odd, it is both even-times even and even-times odd.

**Step 2.** Since A consists of two copies of B, the even number B measures A according to the dyad. The dyad is itself even, being divisible into two equal units. Hence A is even-times even (D7.6, D7.8).

**Step 3.** Starting with A, continue taking halves whenever the current number is even (D7.6). Each half is strictly smaller than the number halved (CN5). Since A is a finite multitude of units, this process must terminate, either at the unit or at a number which is not even (D7.2). It cannot terminate at the unit: reversing the halvings would then obtain A by continually doubling from the dyad, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore it terminates at a number C which is odd (D7.7).

**Step 4.** Starting with the unit, perform exactly as many doublings as there were halvings from A to C, and call the resulting number E. There were at least two halvings, since both A and its first half B are even. In particular, E is a double and is even (D7.6). Now reverse the halvings from C back to A. Starting with one copy of C, each reversal doubles the number of copies; thus the final number of copies is E. Consequently A is the sum of E copies of C, that is, the product of E and C (CN2, D7.15).

**Step 5.** By commutativity of multiplication, A is also the sum of C copies of E (7.16, D7.15). Thus the even number E measures A according to the odd number C, so A is even-times odd (D7.9). Together with Step 2, this proves that A is both even-times even and even-times odd.

## Proposition 9.35
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please be in continued proportion, and there be subtracted from the second and the last numbers equal to the first, then, as the excess of the second is to the first, so will the excess of the last be to all those before it.

**Step 1.** Let a₁, a₂, …, aₙ be the given numbers in continued proportion, so that a₁:a₂ = a₂:a₃ = ⋯ = aₙ₋₁:aₙ. The stipulated excess of the second over the first presupposes a₂ > a₁; consequently the equal successive ratios imply a₁ < a₂ < ⋯ < aₙ. Put d = a₂ − a₁ and e = aₙ − a₁. If there are only two terms, the required proportion is identical on both sides; hence suppose n ≥ 3. [D7.20]

**Step 2.** Put S = a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ₋₁ and T = a₂ + a₃ + ⋯ + aₙ. Since the successive ratios are equal, the ratio of one antecedent to its consequent equals the ratio of all antecedents together to all consequents together. Thus a₁:a₂ = S:T. We choose this numerical summation theorem first because these two shifted sums lead directly to the required excess. [7.12]

**Step 3.** Since aₙ = a₁ + e, adding a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ₋₁ to both sides gives T = S + e. Therefore the remainder after subtracting S from T is precisely e. [CN2]

**Step 4.** Alternating the proportion in Step 2 gives a₂:T = a₁:S. Thus the wholes a₂ and T have the same ratio as the quantities a₁ and S subtracted from them. By the numerical subtraction theorem, their remainders have that same ratio. Consequently d:e = a₁:S. [7.13, 7.11]

**Step 5.** Alternating this last proportion gives d:a₁ = e:S, or explicitly
(a₂ − a₁):a₁ = (aₙ − a₁):(a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ₋₁).
Hence the excess of the second over the first is to the first as the excess of the last over the first is to all the numbers before the last added together. [7.13]

## Proposition 9.36
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be set out continuously in double proportion, until the sum of all becomes prime, and if the sum multiplied into the last make some number, the product will be perfect.

**Step 1.** Write the given progression as a₀ = 1, a₁ = 2, …, aₖ = A, where each term is double its predecessor. Let p = a₀ + a₁ + … + aₖ be prime, and let N = pA be the proposed perfect number. Since the unit is not a prime number, k ≥ 1; consequently A ≥ 2 and p > A. Products here denote repeated addition. [D7.2, D7.11, D7.15, CN5]

**Step 2.** Let B = a₀ + a₁ + … + aₖ₋₁. Doubling these terms gives precisely a₁, a₂, …, aₖ, so p = 1 + 2B. But also p = B + A. Subtracting B from these equal expressions gives A = 1 + B. This obtains the needed summation identity directly from the doubling of the progression. [D7.15, CN2, CN3]

**Step 3.** The dyad is prime, since its only smaller positive measure is the unit. Each term of the progression measures A, by 9.11, with the unit and A itself included directly. Conversely, 9.13 shows that A has no numerical divisor outside this progression. Thus its positive divisors are exactly a₀, a₁, …, aₖ. We choose 9.13 because it applies directly to the given progression with the prime dyad next to the unit, without requiring a general factorization argument. [D7.2, D7.11, D7.15, 9.11, 9.13]

**Step 4.** Consider the following two lists:

(a) a₀, a₁, …, aₖ;

(b) pa₀, pa₁, …, paₖ₋₁.

Every entry measures N: whenever A = aᵢc, multiplication gives N = aᵢ(pc) = (paᵢ)c. Regrouping products follows from repeated addition, and their factors may be interchanged. Every entry in (a) is at most A < N, while every entry in (b) is less than pA = N. Hence all are proper divisors. Each list is strictly increasing, and the lists are disjoint because every entry in (a) is at most A whereas every entry in (b) is at least p > A. [9.11, D7.15, 7.16, CN5]

**Step 5.** To show that these are all the proper divisors, let d > 1 be any proper divisor of N. Write N = de; since d < N, the complementary factor e is also greater than the unit. The prime p measures de, so it measures d or e. [D7.3, D7.15, CN5, 7.30]

**Step 6.** If p measures d, write d = pb, allowing b to be the unit. Then pA = de = p(be), and cancellation gives A = be. Such cancellation is legitimate because, by repeated addition, a greater multiplicand would give a greater product with the same positive multiplier. Thus b is a divisor of A, so Step 3 gives b = aᵢ for some i. Since d = pb < pA, we have b < A and therefore i < k. Hence d occurs in list (b). [D7.15, CN5, 9.13]

**Step 7.** If p measures e, write e = pc, allowing c to be the unit. Then pA = d(pc) = p(dc). Cancelling p as in Step 6 gives A = dc. Thus d measures A and, by Step 3, equals one of a₀, a₁, …, aₖ. Hence d occurs in list (a). The unit already occurs there as a₀, so the two disjoint lists contain every proper divisor of N exactly once. [D7.15, 7.16, CN5, 9.13]

**Step 8.** The sum of list (a) is p, and the sum of list (b) is pB. Therefore the sum of all the proper divisors of N is p + pB = p(1 + B) = pA = N, using A = 1 + B from Step 2. Thus N equals the sum of its own parts and is perfect, as required. [D7.15, CN2, D7.3, D7.22]

# Book 10

## Proposition 10.1
**Statement:** Two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there be subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process be repeated continually, there will be left some magnitude which will be less than the lesser magnitude set out.

**Step 1.** Let A be the greater magnitude and B the lesser. By D5.4, choose a finite multiple nB of B such that nB > A. We use the finite-multiple route: compare this multiple with the total removed, rather than introduce an auxiliary sequence of bisections. [D5.4]

**Step 2.** Put R₀ = A. For each successive subtraction, let Sᵢ be the magnitude removed and Rᵢ the remainder, so that Rᵢ₋₁ = Sᵢ + Rᵢ. We claim that Sᵢ > Rᵢ. Indeed, let Hᵢ be half of Rᵢ₋₁. By the hypothesis, Sᵢ = Hᵢ + Eᵢ for some positive excess Eᵢ. Hence Hᵢ + Hᵢ = Hᵢ + Eᵢ + Rᵢ. Subtracting Hᵢ gives Hᵢ = Eᵢ + Rᵢ. Therefore Sᵢ > Hᵢ > Rᵢ, since each whole is greater than its part. [Hypothesis; CN3; CN5]

**Step 3.** Suppose, for contradiction, that none of the first n remainders is less than B. Then Rᵢ ≥ B for every i from 1 through n. Consequently Sᵢ > B for each of these subtractions. [Step 2]

**Step 4.** Write Sᵢ = B + Fᵢ, where each Fᵢ is positive. Adding these equalities gives
S₁ + ⋯ + Sₙ = nB + (F₁ + ⋯ + Fₙ).
Thus S₁ + ⋯ + Sₙ > nB. But the successive decompositions in Step 2 give
A = S₁ + ⋯ + Sₙ + Rₙ,
so A > S₁ + ⋯ + Sₙ. Therefore A > nB. [Step 2; CN2; CN5]

**Step 5.** This contradicts nB > A from Step 1. Hence at least one of the first n remainders is less than B. Thus, after finitely many of the prescribed subtractions, there is left a magnitude less than the lesser magnitude originally set out. [Steps 1–4]

## Proposition 10.2
**Statement:** If, when the less of two unequal magnitudes is continually subtracted in turn from the greater, that which is left never measures the one before it, the magnitudes will be incommensurable.

**Step 1.** Let A>B be the two magnitudes satisfying the stated subtraction hypothesis. Suppose, for a contradiction, that they are commensurable. Then some positive magnitude E measures both A and B. We take the direct magnitude route, applying 10.1 to alternate remainders. [D10.1.1]

**Step 2.** If E measures two magnitudes X>Y, each consists of a finite number of copies of E. Subtracting Y from X cancels the corresponding copies, so the positive remainder also consists of copies of E. Thus E measures every positive remainder in the prescribed process. In particular, every such remainder is at least E, and E≤B<A. [D5.2; CN3; CN5]

**Step 3.** Group consecutive subtractions of the same lesser magnitude into one turn. Each turn is finite: by Step 2, the magnitude being diminished contains finitely many copies of E, and each subtraction removes at least one copy. Write R₀=A, R₁=B, and let R₂,R₃,… be the successive remainders at the ends of these turns. The hypothesis excludes exact measurement at any turn, so the process continues with positive remainders satisfying
Rᵢ=qᵢRᵢ₊₁+Rᵢ₊₂, where qᵢ≥1 and 0<Rᵢ₊₂<Rᵢ₊₁.
Here qᵢRᵢ₊₁ denotes the copies of Rᵢ₊₁ removed during that turn. [Hypothesis; Step 2; D5.2]

**Step 4.** In each such equality, the removed magnitude qᵢRᵢ₊₁ is at least Rᵢ₊₁ and therefore greater than the remainder Rᵢ₊₂. Consequently Rᵢ>2Rᵢ₊₂: the passage from Rᵢ to Rᵢ₊₂ removes more than half of Rᵢ. Hence the sequence R₀,R₂,R₄,… is obtained by repeatedly subtracting more than half of the current magnitude. [Step 3; CN2; CN5]

**Step 5.** Set out the unequal magnitudes A and E. Since A>E, and the sequence A=R₀,R₂,R₄,… repeatedly removes more than half of what remains, 10.1 gives a remainder R₂ₖ<E after finitely many such passages. [Steps 2 and 4; 10.1]

**Step 6.** But Step 2 shows that E measures R₂ₖ, so R₂ₖ must contain at least one copy of E and cannot be less than E. This contradicts Step 5. Therefore A and B have no common measure and are incommensurable. [D5.2; CN5; D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.3
**Statement:** Given two commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the given commensurable magnitudes, labelled so that A is not less than B. If B measures A, including the case A = B, then B is their greatest common measure: it measures both, and no magnitude greater than B can measure B. Hence suppose that B does not measure A. [D5.2; CN5]

**Step 2.** Starting with A and B, continually subtract the lesser magnitude from the greater, retaining the lesser and the positive remainder as the next pair. Stop as soon as the lesser of the current pair measures the greater. This process must stop: otherwise the successive remainders would never measure their predecessors, and A and B would be incommensurable by 10.2, contrary to the hypothesis and D10.1.1. Denote the terminal pair by H and G, where G measures H. **Path choice:** use 10.2 directly, since its subtraction criterion applies to the given magnitudes without any reduction to numbers. [10.2; D10.1.1]

**Step 3.** The magnitude G measures both members of the terminal pair. Now reverse the subtractions. At any subtraction, if the former pair was X, Y with X > Y, the new pair was Y, X − Y, possibly reordered. If G measures both members of the new pair, then each consists of whole copies of G; adding them shows that G also measures X = Y + (X − Y). Thus G measures both members of the former pair. Repeating this argument backwards through the finite process proves that G measures A and B. [D5.2; CN2]

**Step 4.** Let M be any common measure of A and B. At each subtraction, if M measures X and Y, then X and Y consist of whole copies of M. Subtracting the copies constituting Y from those constituting X leaves whole copies of M constituting X − Y. Therefore M measures both members of the next pair. Following the finite process forwards, M consequently measures G. [D5.2; CN3]

**Step 5.** Since every common measure M of A and B measures G, it is either equal to G or less than G: one copy gives equality, while several copies make G greater than any one of them. No common measure can therefore exceed G. Together with Step 3, this proves that the constructed magnitude G is the greatest common measure of A and B, as required. [D5.2; CN5]

## Proposition 10.4
**Statement:** Given three commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let the three given commensurable magnitudes be A, B, and C. There exists a magnitude H measuring all three [D10.1.1]. Our path is to reduce the problem to the two-magnitude construction [10.3], using successive subtraction on the first pair to keep track of its common measures.

**Step 2.** Starting with A and B, proceed as follows. If they are equal, put D = A. If the lesser measures the greater, put D equal to the lesser. Otherwise subtract the lesser from the greater and continue with the lesser and the remainder, stopping when one measures the other. This process must terminate: otherwise A and B would be incommensurable, contrary to their having the common measure H [10.2, D10.1.1]. Let D be the lesser magnitude in the terminal pair.

**Step 3.** Every common measure of A and B measures D. Indeed, whenever a magnitude K measures two unequal magnitudes X and Y, their difference is also a multiple of K: subtracting the copies of K constituting the lesser from those constituting the greater leaves whole copies of K [D5.2, CN3]. Thus any common measure of the initial pair measures both members of every successive pair, and consequently measures D. In particular, H measures D; since H also measures C, the magnitudes D and C are commensurable [D10.1.1].

**Step 4.** Moreover, D measures A and B. It measures both members of the terminal pair. At each preceding subtraction, the former greater magnitude is the sum of the former lesser magnitude and the remainder. If D measures these two, it measures their sum, by joining their copies of D [D5.2, CN2]. Reversing the finite sequence therefore shows that D measures both original magnitudes. The cases where the process stopped immediately have the same conclusion directly [D5.2].

**Step 5.** Find E, the greatest common measure of D and C [10.3]. Since E measures D, and D measures A and B, replacing each copy of D in A and B by its constituent copies of E shows that E measures A and B [D5.2, CN2]. It also measures C by its construction. Hence E is a common measure of all three given magnitudes.

**Step 6.** Let K be any common measure of A, B, and C. By Step 3, K measures D. Therefore K is a common measure of D and C, and cannot be greater than their greatest common measure E [10.3]. Since E itself measures A, B, and C, it is their greatest common measure. Thus the required magnitude has been found.

## Proposition 10.5
**Statement:** Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be commensurable magnitudes. By D10.1.1, some magnitude C measures both. Thus A consists of k copies of C and B of l copies of C, where k and l are positive repetition counts, possibly one (D5.2). **Path choice:** use this common measure directly; no greatest-common-measure construction is needed.

**Step 2.** Let T be the number consisting of two units. Form M from k copies of T and N from l copies of T. Both M and N are numbers composed of units, even if either repetition count is one (D7.1, D7.2).

**Step 3.** Take arbitrary positive repetition counts r and s. Then rA and rM are equimultiples of A and M, while sB and sN are equimultiples of B and N. By repeated addition, rA consists of rk copies of C and sB of sl copies of C; correspondingly, rM consists of rk copies of T and sN of sl copies of T. Here rk means the total count in r groups of k copies, and similarly for sl (D5.2, D7.2, CN2).

**Step 4.** If rk equals sl, the corresponding sums are equal, so rA = sB and rM = sN (CN2). If rk exceeds sl, rA contains a part equal to sB together with additional copies of C, and rM contains a part equal to sN together with additional copies of T; hence rA > sB and rM > sN (CN2, CN5). If rk falls short of sl, the same argument with the wholes and parts reversed gives rA < sB and rM < sN (CN2, CN5).

**Step 5.** Therefore, for every choice of these equimultiples, rA and rM alike exceed, equal, or fall short of sB and sN respectively. By D5.5, A:B = M:N. Since M and N are numbers, commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.

## Proposition 10.6
**Statement:** If two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be commensurable.

**Step 1.** Let the magnitudes A and B satisfy A:B = m:n, where m and n are numbers, as hypothesized. Regard the numerical terms as finite counts of units; a term arising later may itself be a single unit (D7.1, D7.2). We shall construct a magnitude measuring both A and B, which proves commensurability by D10.1.1.

**Step 2.** Suppose a current pair of magnitudes X,Y and its corresponding numerical pair p,q satisfy X:Y = p:q. Taking single copies in D5.5 shows that X and Y have the same order of size as p and q. Reversing both pairs when necessary also preserves the proportion, directly by D5.5. Thus, whenever the numerical terms are unequal, we may arrange them so that p>q and correspondingly X>Y.

**Step 3.** Replace these pairs by X−Y,Y and p−q,q. Separation of the proportion gives
(X−Y):Y = (p−q):q (5.17).
Both new terms in each pair remain positive. Path choice: separation is the directly applicable ratio operation because it preserves the correspondence after subtracting the lesser term from the greater.

**Step 4.** Repeat Steps 2–3 whenever the numerical terms are unequal. At every subtraction the combined count of units in the numerical pair decreases by the positive count q, while both remaining counts stay positive (D7.1, D7.2, CN5). The initial combined count is finite, so such subtractions cannot continue indefinitely. Since a further subtraction is possible whenever the terms are unequal, the process must reach equal numerical terms.

**Step 5.** Let U,V be the magnitudes corresponding to the terminal numerical pair d,d. The preserved proportion is U:V = d:d. Taking single copies in D5.5 gives U=V. Denote this positive common magnitude by E; the terminal magnitudes are therefore each one copy of E.

**Step 6.** Reverse the finite sequence of subtractions. At any stage, if X−Y consists of r copies of E and Y consists of s copies of E, then adding these equalities shows that X consists of r+s copies of E (CN2). Consequently, being measured by E is preserved at every reversed step (D5.2); any interchange of the two terms plainly leaves this unchanged. Hence the original magnitudes A and B are both measured by E. They are therefore commensurable (D10.1.1), as required.

## Proposition 10.7
**Statement:** Incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be incommensurable magnitudes. Then no magnitude measures both A and B. [D10.1.1]

**Step 2.** Suppose, for contradiction, that A has to B the ratio which some number m has to some number n. Then A and B are commensurable. We apply 10.6 directly because its hypothesis is precisely the assumed equality of ratios. [10.6]

**Step 3.** Since A and B are commensurable, they have a common measure, contrary to Step 1. Therefore no such numbers m and n exist: incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. [D10.1.1; Step 1]

## Proposition 10.9
**Statement:** The squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length. But the squares on straight lines incommensurable in length have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will not have their sides commensurable in length either.

**Step 1.** For any straight line x, write Q(x) for the square constructed on it [1.46]. All such squares are similar: their angles are equal right angles, and their corresponding sides are proportional because each square is equilateral [D1.22, P4, D6.1].

**Step 2.** Suppose that x:y = m:n, where m and n are numbers. Write m² and n² for the square numbers produced by multiplying each number by itself [D7.18]. By 6.20, Q(x):Q(y) is the duplicate ratio of x:y; this theorem applies directly because the figures are similar polygons. By 8.11, m²:n² is the duplicate ratio of m:n. These duplicate ratios are equal: by D5.9, each is the ratio of the extremes of a three-term continued proportion, and 5.22 equates those extreme ratios when the corresponding adjacent ratios are equal. Consequently,
Q(x):Q(y) = m²:n².

**Step 3.** Let a and b be commensurable in length. They therefore have the ratio of a number to a number; say a:b = m:n [10.5]. Applying Step 2 gives Q(a):Q(b) = m²:n². Thus squares on straight lines commensurable in length have the ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 4.** Conversely, suppose that Q(a):Q(b) = m²:n², where m and n are the sides of the given square numbers [D7.18]. Choose a straight line u, and, by laying off successive copies of it, construct c consisting of m copies and d consisting of n copies [P2, P3]. Then c:d = m:n by D5.5: any equimultiples of c and d are compared exactly as the corresponding multiples of their numbers of copies, m and n.

**Step 5.** By Step 2, Q(c):Q(d) = m²:n². Combining this with the hypothesis gives Q(a):Q(b) = Q(c):Q(d) [5.11]. For this reverse passage from square figures to their sides, use the converse direction of 6.22: since the similar figures on the four straight lines are proportional, their corresponding sides are proportional. Hence a:b = c:d. Together with Step 4, this gives a:b = m:n [5.11]. Therefore a and b are commensurable in length [10.6]. This proves the second assertion.

**Step 6.** Now let a and b be incommensurable in length. If Q(a):Q(b) were the ratio of a square number to a square number, Steps 4–5 would make a and b commensurable, contrary to their having no common measure [D10.1.1]. Thus squares on straight lines incommensurable in length do not have the ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 7.** Finally, suppose that Q(a):Q(b) is not the ratio of any square number to any square number. If a and b were commensurable in length, Step 3 would give precisely such a ratio, a contradiction. Hence their sides are incommensurable in length [D10.1.1]. All four assertions follow.

## Proposition 10.10
**Statement:** To find two straight lines incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with an assigned straight line.

**Step 1.** Choose the numerical ratio 2:3 because its consecutive terms give a direct obstruction to its being a ratio of square numbers. Indeed, if two square numbers had this ratio, there would be a mean proportional number between them [8.11], and therefore also a mean proportional number between 2 and 3 [8.8]. Such a number would necessarily be strictly between 2 and 3 [D7.20], which is impossible because numbers are multitudes of units [D7.2]. Thus 2:3 is not the ratio of any square number to any square number.

**Step 2.** Let a be the assigned straight line. Bisect it, and call either half h [1.10]. Produce a beyond one endpoint and, using a circle centred at that endpoint with radius the adjacent half, append another segment equal to h [P2, P3]. Call the resulting whole d. Then a consists of two copies of h and d of three [CN2], so a:d = 2:3 [D5.5].

**Step 3.** Construct a mean proportional b between a and d, and then a mean proportional c between a and b [6.13]. Thus

a:b = b:d, and a:c = c:b.

**Step 4.** Write Q(x) for the square on a straight line x, and R(x,y) for the rectangle contained by x and y [D1.22, D2.1]. The proportions in Step 3 give

Q(b) = R(a,d), and Q(c) = R(a,b) [6.17].

Since Q(a) = R(a,a), comparison of rectangles having the same altitude a gives

Q(a):Q(b) = a:d = 2:3,

Q(a):Q(c) = a:b [6.1, 5.11].

**Step 5.** The squares Q(a) and Q(b) have the numerical ratio 2:3, so they are commensurable [10.6]. Hence a and b are commensurable in square [D10.1.2]. But Step 1 shows that their squares do not have the ratio of a square number to a square number; therefore a and b are incommensurable in length [10.9]. Thus b is incommensurable with a in length only.

**Step 6.** Since a and b are incommensurable in length, a:b is not the ratio of any number to any number [10.7]. By Step 4, the same is true of Q(a):Q(c). Therefore Q(a) and Q(c) are incommensurable [10.8], and consequently a and c are incommensurable in square [D10.1.2].

**Step 7.** Moreover, because Q(a):Q(c) is not any numerical ratio, it is in particular not the ratio of a square number to a square number. Thus a and c are also incommensurable in length [10.9]. The constructed straight lines b and c therefore satisfy the requirements: b is incommensurable with the assigned line a in length only, and c is incommensurable with it in square also.

## Proposition 10.11
**Statement:** If four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be commensurable with the second, the third will also be commensurable with the fourth; and, if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third will also be incommensurable with the fourth.

**Step 1.** Let the four magnitudes A, B, C, D be proportional, so that A:B = C:D. [D5.6]

**Step 2.** Suppose first that A is commensurable with B. Then there are numbers m, n such that A:B = m:n. [10.5] The chosen route begins with 10.5 because commensurability is the given hypothesis, and this proposition expresses it through a numerical ratio.

**Step 3.** Since C:D and m:n have the same ratio as A:B, we have C:D = m:n. [5.11] Therefore C is commensurable with D. [10.6] This proves the first assertion.

**Step 4.** Now suppose that A is incommensurable with B. We reuse the same numerical-ratio criterion by contradiction, rather than introduce a separate criterion. Suppose, contrary to the required conclusion, that C is commensurable with D. Then there are numbers p, q such that C:D = p:q. [10.5]

**Step 5.** Together with A:B = C:D, this gives A:B = p:q. [5.11] Hence A is commensurable with B. [10.6] This contradicts their assumed incommensurability, which excludes any common measure. Consequently C and D cannot have a common measure and are incommensurable. [D10.1.1] Thus both assertions are proved.

## Proposition 10.12
**Statement:** Magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another also.

**Step 1.** Let A and B each be commensurable with the same magnitude C. By 10.5, there are numbers m, n, p, q such that A:C = m:n and C:B = p:q. We choose the numerical-ratio route, arranging a common middle number in order to combine these proportions.

**Step 2.** Let X and Y be the numbers produced when m and n, respectively, multiply p; and let Z be the number produced when n multiplies q. Since m and n multiply the same number p, we have X:Y = m:n by 7.18. Since n multiplies p and q, we have Y:Z = p:q by 7.17.

**Step 3.** The ratios A:C and X:Y are each equal to m:n, and the ratios C:B and Y:Z are each equal to p:q. Therefore A:C = X:Y and C:B = Y:Z, by 5.11.

**Step 4.** Apply 5.22, ex aequali, to the three magnitudes A, C, B and the three numbers X, Y, Z. It follows that A:B = X:Z.

**Step 5.** Since A and B have the ratio of the number X to the number Z, they are commensurable by 10.6. This criterion applies directly to the numerical ratio just obtained. Thus magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another.

## Proposition 10.13
**Statement:** If two magnitudes be commensurable, and the one of them be incommensurable with any magnitude, the remaining one will also be incommensurable with the same.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be commensurable, and let A be incommensurable with C. Thus A and C have no common measure. We must prove that B and C are incommensurable. (Hypotheses; D10.1.1.)

**Step 2.** Choose contradiction using 10.12, since it applies directly to magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude. Suppose B and C are commensurable. Then C is commensurable with B, because a common measure measures both magnitudes regardless of their order. (D10.1.1.)

**Step 3.** A is commensurable with B by hypothesis, and C is commensurable with B by Step 2. Therefore A and C are commensurable with one another. (10.12.)

**Step 4.** Consequently A and C have a common measure, contradicting Step 1. Hence B and C cannot have a common measure and are therefore incommensurable, as required. (D10.1.1.)

## Proposition 10.14
**Statement:** If four straight lines be proportional, and the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line commensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by  the square on a straight line commensurable with the third. And, if the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by the square on a straight line in-commensurable with the third.

**Step 1.** Let the four straight lines be a, b, c, d, with a:b = c:d. Denote the square on a straight line x by S(x), constructing the squares as necessary by 1.46. Let e be the straight line given in the hypothesis, so that S(a) = S(b) + S(e).

**Step 2.** Since a:b = c:d, the squares on these lines are proportional: S(a):S(b) = S(c):S(d) [6.22]. Since S(a) is greater than S(b) by hypothesis, S(c) is greater than S(d) [5.14].

**Step 3.** Construct a square equal to the positive rectilineal excess of S(c) over S(d), and let its side be f [2.14]. Thus S(c) = S(d) + S(f).

**Step 4.** Alternating the proportion in Step 2 gives S(a):S(c) = S(b):S(d) [5.16]. Consequently, the whole areas have the same ratio as the areas taken away. Their remainders therefore have that same ratio: S(a):S(c) = S(e):S(f) [5.19]. Alternating again gives S(a):S(e) = S(c):S(f) [5.16].

**Step 5.** By the converse of 6.22, the sides of these proportional squares are proportional: a:e = c:f. This is the direct path: the proportion already obtained between squares yields the required proportion between straight lines, without introducing ratios of square numbers.

**Step 6.** If e is commensurable with a, then, from a:e = c:f, the straight line f is commensurable with c [10.11]. Together with S(c) = S(d) + S(f) from Step 3, this proves the first assertion.

**Step 7.** If e is incommensurable with a, then the same proportion a:e = c:f shows that f is incommensurable with c [10.11]. Again S(c) = S(d) + S(f), so the square on c exceeds the square on d by the square on a straight line incommensurable with c. This proves the second assertion and completes the proof.
